// ewSpectrum kicks one uniform gauge direction and returns its frequency.
// Uniform (k=0) fields have exactly zero Laplacian and zero gradient on any
// lattice, so these mass measurements carry no discretization error at all --
// a 4^3 box gives the same answer as 64^3.
func ewSpectrum(t *testing.T, eps float32, nsteps int,
	kick func(ss *Sim), probe func() float32) (float64, float64) {
	ss := ewSim(4)
	kick(ss)
	ewWrap()
	y := make([]float64, nsteps)
	peak := 0.0
	for i := range nsteps {
		ewStep(ss)
		y[i] = float64(probe())
		peak = math.Max(peak, math.Abs(y[i]))
	}
	return freqZC(y), peak
}

// TestGaugeBosonMasses is the acceptance test for the whole gauge sector.
// No mass term appears anywhere in the kernel: these frequencies are produced
// entirely by the Higgs current evaluated at the vacuum.
func TestGaugeBosonMasses(t *testing.T) {
	p := &Params[0]
	p.Defaults()
	c := float64(p.C)
	g, gp := float64(p.GW), float64(p.GpW)
	n := math.Hypot(g, gp)
	eps := float32(1e-4)
	nsteps := 3000

	t.Logf("v=%.6f  m_W=%.6f  m_Z=%.6f  theta_W=%.4f deg  (all per cube)",
		p.HiggsV, p.MW, p.MZ, math.Atan2(gp, g)*180/math.Pi)

	// --- W: kick W^1 in the X direction -----------------------------------
	wantW := c * float64(p.MW)
	gotW, _ := ewSpectrum(t, eps, nsteps,
		func(ss *Sim) { ss.Fill(EWW1Xs, Both, eps) },
		func() float32 { return ewGet(EWW1Xv) })
	t.Logf("W       : omega = %.6f  want c*m_W = %.6f  ratio %.5f", gotW, wantW, gotW/wantW)
	if math.Abs(gotW/wantW-1) > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("W frequency %g, want %g", gotW, wantW)
	}

	// --- Z: the (W^3, B) combination (g, -g')/N ----------------------------
	cw3, cb := float32(g/n), float32(-gp/n)
	wantZ := c * float64(p.MZ)
	gotZ, _ := ewSpectrum(t, eps, nsteps,
		func(ss *Sim) {
			ss.Fill(EWW3Xs, Both, cw3*eps)
			ss.Fill(EWBXs, Both, cb*eps)
		},
		func() float32 { return cw3*ewGet(EWW3Xv) + cb*ewGet(EWBXv) })
	t.Logf("Z       : omega = %.6f  want c*m_Z = %.6f  ratio %.5f", gotZ, wantZ, gotZ/wantZ)
	if math.Abs(gotZ/wantZ-1) > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("Z frequency %g, want %g", gotZ, wantZ)
	}

	// --- photon: the orthogonal combination (g', g)/N ----------------------
	// Q = T^3 + Y annihilates the vacuum, so this direction must be EXACTLY
	// flat: not approximately massless, but zero force to machine precision.
	aw3, ab := float32(gp/n), float32(g/n)
	gotA, peakA := ewSpectrum(t, eps, nsteps,
		func(ss *Sim) {
			ss.Fill(EWW3Xs, Both, aw3*eps)
			ss.Fill(EWBXs, Both, ab*eps)
		},
		func() float32 { return aw3*ewGet(EWW3Xv) + ab*ewGet(EWBXv) })
	t.Logf("photon  : omega = %.6f  want 0 (exactly flat); peak |velocity| = %.3e", gotA, peakA)
	if gotA != 0 || peakA != 0 {
		t.Errorf("photon direction is not flat: omega %g, peak velocity %g", gotA, peakA)
	}

	t.Logf("check   : m_W/(m_Z cos theta_W) = %.6f  (rho parameter, must be 1)",
		float64(p.MW)/(float64(p.MZ)*math.Cos(math.Atan2(gp, g))))
}

## The design

The whole gauge coupling collapses to **one operation**, $-i\mathcal{G}\Psi$, in [electroweak.goal](../wavesim/electroweak.goal):

```go
func EWGaugeAct(w1, w2, w3, b float32, psi math32.Vector4) math32.Vector4
```

where $\mathcal{G} = gW^aT^a + g'Y_\Phi B$ written out in real components. Everything else composes from it. The covariant derivative is just $D_\mu\Psi = \partial_\mu\Psi + \texttt{EWGaugeAct}(W_\mu, B_\mu, \Psi)$, and the covariant Laplacian falls out by applying the same function to three different arguments:

$$D_jD_j\Psi = \nabla^2\Psi \underbrace{-\,i(\partial_j\mathcal{G}_j)\Psi}_{\text{act on }\Psi} \underbrace{-\,i\mathcal{G}_j\partial_j\Psi}_{\text{act on }\partial_j\Psi} \underbrace{-\,i\mathcal{G}_j D_j\Psi}_{\text{act on }D_j\Psi}$$

```go
cov := EWAdd4(lap, EWGaugeAct(dvW1, dvW2, dvW3, dvB, psi))
cov = EWAdd4(cov, EWGaugeAct(w1x, w2x, w3x, bx, EWAdd4(dxp, dX)))
// ... y, z
```

The currents go through `EWCurrent`, and each four-potential advances by `EWGaugeStep` solving $\Box W^a_\mu = j^a_\mu$ — structurally identical to your `MaxwellKernel`, Lorenz gauge, with the electroweak current swapped in. **No mass term appears anywhere in the kernel.** The masses come out of the current being proportional to $-m^2 W$ once $\Psi \neq 0$ everywhere.

Added `GW` / `GpW` to `Parameters` (free, exploration-side) with `MW` / `MZ` as derived reference values, and the SM numbers on the `Units` side.

The photon line is the one that proves the group theory is right rather than just the arithmetic: the same kick, in the direction $Q = T^3 + Y$ annihilates, produces literally nothing — eleven orders below the W. That only happens if the relative sign of $W^3$ on the two diagonal entries and the $Y_\Phi = +1/2$ on both are exactly right. The earlier Higgs tests still pass unchanged.

The $k=0$ measurement is exact, not approximate: uniform fields have identically zero Laplacian and gradient, so a $4^3$ box gives the same answer as $64^3$.

## What I left out, deliberately

**The Yang–Mills self-coupling.** In Lorenz gauge the full non-abelian equation carries three more terms beyond $\Box W = j$:

$$2g\varepsilon^{abc}W^b_\mu\partial^\mu W^c_\nu \;-\; g\varepsilon^{abc}W^b_\mu\partial_\nu W^{c\mu} \;+\; g^2\varepsilon^{abc}\varepsilon^{cde}W^b_\mu W^{d\mu}W^e_\nu$$

All three are quadratic or cubic in $W$, so they vanish at linear order and contribute nothing to the spectrum above — those numbers are exact without them. What they provide is the W self-interaction, i.e. the difference between real SU(2) and three independent copies of U(1). The equations are written into the kernel doc comment. Worth adding before anything with large-amplitude W fields.

One honest caveat: the $\mathcal{G}_0$ terms in the Higgs equation are implemented, but the test only exercises them at second order (the Higgs back-reaction sources $W_0$ weakly). Their relative sign isn't independently pinned down yet. A good next test would be a global phase rotation of the doublet, which sources $W_0$/$B_0$ directly.

// TestGaugeTimeComponent isolates the time-component (G_0) sector.
//
// A constant uniform B_0 over a vacuum Higgs is PURE GAUGE: it is the same
// physical state as a vacuum whose phase turns at a constant rate. The exact
// solution has D_0 Psi = 0 identically, which means
//
//	d_t Psi = -c * EWGaugeAct(B_0, Psi)
//
// i.e. the neutral component rotates in the (hs0a, hs0b) plane at
//
//	omega = c * g' * Y_Phi * B_0 = c * g' * B_0 / 2
//
// with |Phi| EXACTLY constant. Nothing else in the kernel can produce this
// motion: every spatial gradient, every spatial current and the potential
// force all vanish identically here, so it comes entirely from the three G_0
// terms. Get their sign or magnitude wrong and the radius spirals instead of
// holding, which is why this is the test that pins them down.
func TestGaugeTimeComponent(t *testing.T) {
	ss := ewSim(4)
	p := ss.Params
	b := float32(0.2)
	v := p.HiggsV
	om := float64(p.C) * float64(p.GpW) * float64(b) / 2.0
	nsteps := int(8 * 2 * math.Pi / om)

	ss.Fill(EWB0s, Both, b)
	ss.Fill(EWHv0b, Both, float32(om)*v) // the velocity making D_0 Psi = 0
	ewWrap()

	mag0 := float64(v) * float64(v)
	y := make([]float64, nsteps)
	magLo, magHi := math.Inf(1), math.Inf(-1)
	b0Lo, b0Hi := math.Inf(1), math.Inf(-1)
	for i := range nsteps {
		ewStep(ss)
		y[i] = float64(ewGet(EWHs0b))
		m := float64(ewGet(EWHmag))
		magLo, magHi = math.Min(magLo, m), math.Max(magHi, m)
		bb := float64(ewGet(EWB0s))
		b0Lo, b0Hi = math.Min(b0Lo, bb), math.Max(b0Hi, bb)
	}
	got := freqZC(y)
	t.Logf("rotation : omega = %.6f  want c*g'*B0/2 = %.6f  ratio %.5f", got, om, got/om)
	t.Logf("radius   : mag in [%.8f, %.8f] vs v^2 = %.8f -- drift %.2e relative",
		magLo, magHi, mag0, (magHi-magLo)/mag0)
	t.Logf("B0       : stays in [%.8f, %.8f] (pure gauge, must not evolve)", b0Lo, b0Hi)

	if math.Abs(got/om-1) > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("phase rotation %g, want %g", got, om)
	}
	// |Phi| must hold: a sign error in the G_0 terms shows up here first.
	if (magHi-magLo)/mag0 > 1e-4 {
		t.Errorf("|Phi| not conserved: mag range [%g, %g], v^2 = %g", magLo, magHi, mag0)
	}
	if math.Abs(b0Hi-float64(b)) > 1e-6 || math.Abs(b0Lo-float64(b)) > 1e-6 {
		t.Errorf("B0 evolved away from %g: [%g, %g]", b, b0Lo, b0Hi)
	}
}
GOEOF

import math
# A constant A_0 is exactly a rotating frame: the kernel's three G_0 terms give
#    acc = -2w (vy, -vx) + w^2 (x, y)      <- Coriolis + centrifugal
# whose exact solution is pure rotation at w. Integrate it with the kernel's
# own scheme (symplectic Euler) and see whether the radius drift is the scheme.
def run(w, v, n):
    x, y, vx, vy = v, 0.0, 0.0, w*v
    r0 = v*v
    lo = hi = r0
    for _ in range(n):
        ax = -2*w*vy + w*w*x
        ay =  2*w*vx + w*w*y
        vx += ax; vy += ay
        x += vx;  y += vy
        r = x*x + y*y
        lo, hi = min(lo, r), max(hi, r)
    return (x*x+y*y)/r0, lo/r0, hi/r0

Physics is right — it's the integrator. The three $\mathcal{G}_0$ terms produce exactly

$$\ddot{x} = -2\omega\dot{y} + \omega^2 x, \qquad \ddot{y} = +2\omega\dot{x} + \omega^2 y$$

the **rotating-frame** equation (Coriolis + centrifugal), whose exact solution is pure rotation — which *is* the statement that a constant $A_0$ is pure gauge. Symplectic Euler doesn't conserve radius against a velocity-dependent force, and the drift scales as exactly $\omega^2$ per step (`/omega^2` column = 1.0000). So the test should be a convergence check, not an equality.

Done. First, the correction from last turn: the $\mathcal{G}_0$ terms weren't merely untested — they were **absent**. `a0`/`d0` fed only `EWCurrent`, so the Higgs sourced $W_0$/$B_0$ but never felt them back. That's now fixed in [electroweak.goal](../wavesim/electroweak.goal):

```go
q0 := EWGaugeAct(oc*w10v, oc*w20v, oc*w30v, oc*b0v, psi)  // (1/c)(d_t G_0) Psi
q1 := EWGaugeAct(w10, w20, w30, b0, dtp)                  // (1/c) G_0 d_t Psi
q2 := EWGaugeAct(w10, w20, w30, b0, d0)                   // G_0 D_0 Psi
cov = cov - q0 - q1 - q2
```

Same compositional structure as the spatial sector — three more applications of the one gauge operation.

## The test

A constant uniform $B_0$ over a vacuum Higgs is **pure gauge**: identical to a vacuum whose phase turns at a fixed rate. Every spatial gradient, every spatial current and the potential force vanish identically, so any motion at all comes solely from the $\mathcal{G}_0$ terms. Initialize the velocity that makes $D_0\Psi = 0$ and the prediction is rotation at exactly $\omega = c\,g' B_0/2$ with $|\Phi|$ constant.

Writing the three terms out, they give

$$\ddot{x} = -2\omega\dot{y} + \omega^2 x, \qquad \ddot{y} = +2\omega\dot{x} + \omega^2 y$$

the **rotating-frame equation** — Coriolis plus centrifugal. That's the mechanical content of "a constant $A_0$ is a change of frame, not a force," and the kernel reproduces it without being told to.

```
      B0      omega     measured     ratio    drift/step      x4?
   0.200   0.017500     0.017697   1.01124     1.371e-04         
   0.100   0.008750     0.008814   1.00733     3.510e-05     3.91
   0.050   0.004375     0.004406   1.00709     8.812e-06     3.98
```

The radius drift converges as $O(\omega^2)$ — 3.91, 3.98 against a target of 4 — which is the signature of discretization rather than a physics error. That's the sharp assertion; a sign error would make the radius grow immediately and the rate come out wrong. The residual ~1% on the rate is the scheme's own $O(\omega)$ phase error, which I reproduced independently in a standalone model of the integrator (1.0103 / 1.0052 / 1.0026, halving with $\omega$), so the tolerance is set knowingly rather than fitted.

## A real limitation this surfaced

My first version of the test ran two full periods and returned `NaN`. That isn't a bug in the kernel — it's that **the rotating-frame system is only marginally stable** (degenerate eigenvalues $\pm i\omega$), so any explicit integrator drives it. Under symplectic Euler the radius grows exponentially, roughly doubling once per rotation period:

```
step  360  radius/v = 0.9957      step 1800  radius/v =  15.26
step  720  radius/v = 1.6240      step 3600  radius/v = 531.86
```

The cause is that the Coriolis term is velocity-dependent, which symplectic Euler does not handle symplectically. So **sustained large $A_0$ over many periods is not yet trustworthy** in this kernel. It's recorded in the test's doc comment. If that regime matters, the fix is a velocity-dependent-force integrator (Boris push, or the standard trick for magnetic forces in PIC codes) rather than anything in the physics.

Also worth noting: `NaN` silently passed my first assertion, since `NaN > 0.02` is false. There's now an explicit `math.IsNaN` guard.

All 5 tests pass, 14 shader validations clean, gofmt/vet/build clean. Yang–Mills self-coupling next?

Your version is strictly better — `.Add(...)` compiles to native `dxp+(ax)` on `vec4<f32>`, so the GPU does it as one hardware vector op instead of a function call with four scalar adds. Good to know for Yang–Mills, where there'll be a lot more of this.

One thing worth flagging: **the WGSL was stale.** `EWAdd4`/`EWVec4` were gone from the source but still defined and called in `shaders/ElectroweakKernel.wgsl`, so the GPU path was running the old kernel. The native Go tests can't catch that — they execute the transpiled `.go`, never the shader. I've regenerated (`goal build` then `go generate ./...`); 14 validations pass, helpers gone, tests still green.

That's a general trap with this setup: a source edit plus a green `go test` doesn't mean the GPU path is current. Only `go generate` closes that gap.

import numpy as np, itertools, math

# ---- replicate Gradient18 exactly -----------------------------------------
# For each direction, 9 antipodal PAIRS indexed by the two transverse offsets:
#   minus = (-1, a, b)   plus = (+1, -a, -b)   weight = 1/|n|, |n|=sqrt(1+a^2+b^2)
TRANS = [(a, b) for b in (-1, 0, 1) for a in (-1, 0, 1)]

def stencil(wfun):
    """Return (offsets e_j for the +x direction, weights) normalised so
    the gradient of a linear function is exact."""
    es, ws = [], []
    for a, b in TRANS:
        es.append(np.array([1.0, -a, -b]))
        ws.append(wfun(math.sqrt(1 + a*a + b*b)))
    ws = np.array(ws)
    ws = ws / (2.0 * ws.sum())     # so 2*sum(w) = 1
    return np.array(es), ws

G18  = stencil(lambda d: 1.0/d)            # what the code does
CD   = stencil(lambda d: 1.0 if d == 1 else 0.0)   # plain central difference
# D3Q27 lattice-Boltzmann gradient weights, face:edge:corner = 16:4:1
ISO  = stencil(lambda d: {1.0: 16.0, math.sqrt(2): 4.0, math.sqrt(3): 1.0}[round(d,9) if False else (1.0 if abs(d-1)<1e-9 else (math.sqrt(2) if abs(d-math.sqrt(2))<1e-9 else math.sqrt(3)))])

NAMES = [("Gradient18  (1/d)", G18), ("central diff  (7pt)", CD), ("isotropic  (16:4:1)", ISO)]

import numpy as np, itertools, math
rng=np.random.default_rng(1)
dirs=[d/np.linalg.norm(d) for d in rng.standard_normal((3000,3))]
offs=[np.array(o,dtype=float) for o in itertools.product((-1,0,1),repeat=3) if any(o)]

def lapw(c1,c2,c3):
    return np.array([{1:c1,2:c2,3:c3}[int(o@o)] for o in offs])

def lspread(w,kmag):
    rs=[(-sum(wi*(math.cos((kmag*d)@o)-1.0) for wi,o in zip(w,offs)))/(kmag*kmag) for d in dirs]
    return min(rs),max(rs)

    n=sum(wi*o[0]**2 for wi,o in zip(w,offs))

TRANS=[(a,b) for b in (-1,0,1) for a in (-1,0,1)]
def mk(c1,c2,cc):

    for a,b in TRANS:
        d2=1+a*a+b*b; ws.append(c1 if d2==1 else (c2 if d2==2 else cc))
        es.append(np.array([1.0,-a,-b]))
    ws=np.array(ws); return np.array(es), ws/(2*ws.sum())
def gspread(st,kmag):

Good news and bad news. The **normalization is exactly right** — which is the hard part — but the weighting isn't isotropic, and there's a clean fix.

## What's right

```
[1] gradient of a linear function a.r  (must be exactly a):
  Gradient18  (1/d)      max error 4.441e-16
```

Exact on linear functions for arbitrary directions. And because every stencil point is paired with its exact antipode $(-1,a,b) \leftrightarrow (+1,-a,-b)$, all **even**-order error terms cancel identically, so it's genuinely 2nd-order accurate — same order as a central difference. That pairing is the structurally important choice and you got it right.

## What's off

The leading (3rd-order) error is $\tfrac13 T^{abc}\partial_a\partial_b\partial_c f$ with $T^{abc} = \sum_j w_j e_j^a e_j^b e_j^c$. For that error to be isotropic it must be proportional to $\partial_x\nabla^2 f$, which requires $T^{111} = 3T^{122}$:

```
[2] isotropic iff T111 == 3*T122:
  Gradient18  (1/d)      T111=0.500000  3*T122=0.910000   ratio 1.8200
  central diff  (7pt)    T111=0.500000  3*T122=0.000000   ratio 0.0000
  isotropic  (16:4:1)    T111=0.500000  3*T122=0.500000   ratio 1.0000
```

Gradient18 overshoots by 82%; the central difference undershoots by 100%. So your intuition pushed in exactly the right direction — just about twice too far. In plane-wave terms:

```
[3] |k_eff|/|k| spread over 4000 random directions
    Gradient18  (1/d)    0.8015% @|k|=0.3    5.0395% @|k|=0.8
    central diff  (7pt)  0.9927% @|k|=0.3    6.8080% @|k|=0.8
    isotropic 16:4:1     0.0040% @|k|=0.3    0.1899% @|k|=0.8
```

Gradient18 beats the central difference, but only by ~1.3×, where the right weights give **200× at low $k$**.

## The one thing you can't fix, and the one you can

$T^{111} = \sum_j w_j = 1/2$ is pinned by the normalization, because every pair sits at $x = \pm1$ regardless of weighting. So the **magnitude** error is identical for every member of this stencil family — all three give $|k_{\rm eff}|/|k| = 0.8967$ at $|k|=0.8$. You cannot buy accuracy by reweighting; you can only buy isotropy. That's worth knowing before tuning anything.

The isotropy condition works out to a one-parameter family (with $c_1, c_2, c_3$ the face/edge/corner pair weights):

$$c_1 = 2c_2 + 8c_3, \qquad c_1 + 4c_2 + 4c_3 = \tfrac12 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c_1 = \tfrac16 + 4c_3,\;\; c_2 = \tfrac1{12} - 2c_3$$

The tidiest member is **face : edge : corner = 16 : 4 : 1** ($c = 2/9,\ 1/18,\ 1/72$) — which is exactly the D3Q27 lattice-Boltzmann gradient weighting, an independent confirmation that the condition is the right one. Against your current $1 : 1/\sqrt2 : 1/\sqrt3 \approx 1.73 : 1.22 : 1$, the corners are massively over-weighted. A cheaper variant, $2:1:0$, drops the corners entirely and is marginally better still (0.161% vs 0.190% at $|k|=0.8$).

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"math/rand/v2"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

// Tests for the 26/18-neighbor stencils. Each one is checked on two levels:
// that the WEIGHTS satisfy the normalization and isotropy identities, and that
// the actual Laplacian26 / Gradient18 code paths reproduce known derivatives.
//
// The normalization conditions make a stencil correct. The isotropy conditions
// make its leading error direction-independent, which is the whole point of
// using 26 neighbors instead of 6 -- a stencil can be perfectly normalized and
// still be badly anisotropic, which is exactly what 1/d^2 (Laplacian) and 1/d
// (gradient) weighting are.

const stSize = 6 // interior cells per side; full array is stSize+2

func stencilSim() *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU = false
	ss.Config.GUI = false
	ss.Config.Equation = Electroweak
	ss.Config.Size.Set(stSize, stSize, stSize)
	ss.ConfigVars()
	ss.Params = &Params[0]
	ss.StateVars = EWStatesN
	ss.ConfigState()
	GetCtx(0).Init()
	State.SetZeros()
	return ss
}

// stCtr is the cell the stencils are evaluated at; fill uses coordinates
// relative to it so the analytic derivatives are evaluated at the origin.
const stCtr = (stSize + 2) / 2

// stFill writes f(x,y,z) into state variable v over the WHOLE array, edges
// included, so the stencil at stCtr has real values in every neighbor.
func stFill(v int32, f func(x, y, z float64) float64) {
	n := stSize + 2
	for z := range n {
		for y := range n {
			for x := range n {
				State.Set(float32(f(float64(x-stCtr), float64(y-stCtr), float64(z-stCtr))),
					z, y, x, int(v), 0)
			}
		}
	}
}

func stLap(v int32) float64 {
	c := int32(stCtr)
	return float64(Laplacian26(c, c, c, v, 0, State.Value(stCtr, stCtr, stCtr, int(v), 0)))
}

func stGrad(v int32) math32.Vector3 {
	c := int32(stCtr)
	return Gradient18(c, c, c, v, 0)
}

// --- Laplacian26 -----------------------------------------------------------

func TestLaplacian26Exact(t *testing.T) {
	stencilSim()
	v := int32(EWHsCa)
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name string
		f    func(x, y, z float64) float64
		want float64
	}{
		{"constant", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return 3 }, 0},
		{"linear x", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return x }, 0},
		{"x^2", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return x * x }, 2},
		{"r^2", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return x*x + y*y + z*z }, 6},
		{"xy", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return x * y }, 0},
		// the quadratic anisotropy: a stencil with the wrong second moments
		// returns something non-zero here
		{"2x^2-y^2-z^2", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return 2*x*x - y*y - z*z }, 0},
	} {
		stFill(v, tc.f)
		if got := stLap(v); math.Abs(got-tc.want) > 1e-6 {
			t.Errorf("lap(%s) = %g, want %g", tc.name, got, tc.want)
		}
	}
}

// TestLaplacian26Isotropy checks the two weight identities directly.
func TestLaplacian26Isotropy(t *testing.T) {
	stencilSim()
	var norm, q4, q22 float64
	for j := range 26 {
		w := float64(NeighWts.Value(int(LaplacianWts), j))
		dx := float64(NeighOffs.Value(j, int(math32.X)))
		dy := float64(NeighOffs.Value(j, int(math32.Y)))
		norm += w * dx * dx
		q4 += w * dx * dx * dx * dx
		q22 += w * dx * dx * dy * dy
	}
	t.Logf("sum w dx^2 = %.6f (want 2)   sum w dx^4 = %.6f   3*sum w dx^2dy^2 = %.6f", norm, q4, 3*q22)
	if math.Abs(norm-2) > 1e-6 {
		t.Errorf("normalization sum w dx^2 = %g, want 2", norm)
	}
	if math.Abs(3*q22/q4-1) > 1e-6 {
		t.Errorf("4th-order isotropy: 3*sum w dx^2dy^2 / sum w dx^4 = %g, want 1", 3*q22/q4)
	}
}

// --- Gradient18 ------------------------------------------------------------

func TestGradient18Exact(t *testing.T) {
	stencilSim()
	v := int32(EWHsCa)
	rng := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2))
	worst := 0.0
	for range 100 { // gradient of a.r must be exactly a, in any direction
		a := [3]float64{rng.NormFloat64(), rng.NormFloat64(), rng.NormFloat64()}
		stFill(v, func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return a[0]*x + a[1]*y + a[2]*z })
		g := stGrad(v)
		for i, gi := range []float32{g.X, g.Y, g.Z} {
			worst = math.Max(worst, math.Abs(float64(gi)-a[i]))
		}
	}
	t.Logf("gradient of a linear function: max error %.3e", worst)
	if worst > 1e-5 {
		t.Errorf("gradient not exact on linear functions: max error %g", worst)
	}
	// even functions must give exactly zero (the stencil is antipodal, so all
	// even-order error terms cancel -- that is what makes it 2nd order)
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name string
		f    func(x, y, z float64) float64
	}{
		{"x^2", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return x * x }},
		{"xy", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return x * y }},
		{"r^2", func(x, y, z float64) float64 { return x*x + y*y + z*z }},
	} {
		stFill(v, tc.f)
		g := stGrad(v)
		if m := math.Max(math.Abs(float64(g.X)), math.Max(math.Abs(float64(g.Y)),
			math.Abs(float64(g.Z)))); m > 1e-6 {
			t.Errorf("grad(%s) at origin = %v, want 0 (antipodal pairing)", tc.name, g)
		}
	}
}

// TestGradient18Isotropy checks the weight identities for the +x stencil.
// Note sum_j w_j is pinned at 1/2 by the normalization for ANY ratios, since
// every pair sits at x = +-1: only the isotropy is tunable.
func TestGradient18Isotropy(t *testing.T) {
	stencilSim()
	var t111, t122 float64
	for j := range 9 {
		w := float64(NeighWts.Value(int(Grad18Wts), j))
		ex := float64(FaceOffs.Value(int(math32.X), int(Plus1), j, int(math32.X)))
		ey := float64(FaceOffs.Value(int(math32.X), int(Plus1), j, int(math32.Y)))
		t111 += w * ex * ex * ex
		t122 += w * ex * ey * ey
	}
	t.Logf("T111 = %.6f (want 0.5)   3*T122 = %.6f", t111, 3*t122)
	if math.Abs(t111-0.5) > 1e-6 {
		t.Errorf("normalization T111 = %g, want 0.5", t111)
	}
	if math.Abs(3*t122/t111-1) > 1e-6 {
		t.Errorf("3rd-order isotropy: 3*T122/T111 = %g, want 1", 3*t122/t111)
	}
}

// --- plane-wave anisotropy, the end-to-end statement -----------------------

// TestStencilPlaneWaveIsotropy sweeps wave directions and bounds how much the
// effective wavenumber each stencil reports varies with direction. This is the
// quantity that actually matters: it is the directional spread of the wave
// dispersion relation, i.e. how much faster a wave travels along a lattice
// diagonal than along an axis.
func TestStencilPlaneWaveIsotropy(t *testing.T) {
	stencilSim()
	rng := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(3, 4))
	dirs := make([][3]float64, 2000)
	for i := range dirs {
		d := [3]float64{rng.NormFloat64(), rng.NormFloat64(), rng.NormFloat64()}
		n := math.Sqrt(d[0]*d[0] + d[1]*d[1] + d[2]*d[2])
		dirs[i] = [3]float64{d[0] / n, d[1] / n, d[2] / n}
	}
	for _, km := range []float64{0.3, 0.8} {
		lapLo, lapHi := math.Inf(1), math.Inf(-1)
		grdLo, grdHi := math.Inf(1), math.Inf(-1)
		for _, d := range dirs {
			k := [3]float64{km * d[0], km * d[1], km * d[2]}
			// Laplacian: returns -k_eff^2 on exp(i k.r)
			s := 0.0
			for j := range 26 {
				w := float64(NeighWts.Value(int(LaplacianWts), j))
				ph := 0.0
				for a := range 3 {
					ph += k[a] * float64(NeighOffs.Value(j, a))
				}
				s += w * (math.Cos(ph) - 1)
			}
			r := -s / (km * km)
			lapLo, lapHi = math.Min(lapLo, r), math.Max(lapHi, r)
			// Gradient: returns i*k_eff
			var ke [3]float64
			for ax := range 3 {
				g := 0.0
				for j := range 9 {
					w := float64(NeighWts.Value(int(Grad18Wts), j))
					ph := 0.0
					for a := range 3 {
						ph += k[a] * float64(FaceOffs.Value(ax, int(Plus1), j, a))
					}
					g += w * 2 * math.Sin(ph)
				}
				ke[ax] = g
			}
			r = math.Sqrt(ke[0]*ke[0]+ke[1]*ke[1]+ke[2]*ke[2]) / km
			grdLo, grdHi = math.Min(grdLo, r), math.Max(grdHi, r)
		}
		lapSp, grdSp := 100*(lapHi-lapLo), 100*(grdHi-grdLo)
		t.Logf("|k|=%.1f  Laplacian26 spread %.4f%%   Gradient18 spread %.4f%%", km, lapSp, grdSp)
		// Bounds are ~3x the measured isotropic values, well under the 1.97%
		// and 5.04% that the 1/d^2 and 1/d weightings produced at |k|=0.8.

cat >> funcs_test.go <<'GOEOF'

// TestLaplacian26CFL pins the stability limit. The leapfrog update is stable
// while C^2 |lambda_min| < 4, where lambda_min is the most negative eigenvalue
// of the stencil. For the isotropic weights that is exactly -16/3, attained at
// k = (pi, pi, 0), so C must stay below sqrt(3)/2.
//
// The older anisotropic 1/d^2 weighting had lambda_min = -4 exactly and so
// allowed C < 1: isotropy costs about 13% of the timestep. If this test starts
// failing after a weight change, the C limit in Parameters needs updating with
// it.
func TestLaplacian26CFL(t *testing.T) {
	stencilSim()
	eig := func(k [3]float64) float64 {
		s := 0.0
		for j := range 26 {
			w := float64(NeighWts.Value(int(LaplacianWts), j))
			ph := 0.0
			for a := range 3 {
				ph += k[a] * float64(NeighOffs.Value(j, a))
			}
			s += w * (math.Cos(ph) - 1)
		}
		return s
	}
	const n = 60
	worst := 0.0
	for i := range n + 1 {
		for j := range n + 1 {
			for l := range n + 1 {
				k := [3]float64{math.Pi * float64(i) / n, math.Pi * float64(j) / n,
					math.Pi * float64(l) / n}
				worst = math.Min(worst, eig(k))
			}
		}
	}
	atCorner := eig([3]float64{math.Pi, math.Pi, 0})
	cMax := 2 / math.Sqrt(-worst)
	t.Logf("lambda_min = %.6f (want -16/3 = %.6f, attained at k=(pi,pi,0): %.6f)",
		worst, -16.0/3.0, atCorner)
	t.Logf("CFL limit: C < %.6f (sqrt(3)/2 = %.6f)", cMax, math.Sqrt(3)/2)
	if math.Abs(worst+16.0/3.0) > 1e-9 {
		t.Errorf("spectral radius %g, want -16/3 = %g", worst, -16.0/3.0)
	}
	if math.Abs(cMax-math.Sqrt(3)/2) > 1e-9 {
		t.Errorf("CFL limit %g, want sqrt(3)/2 = %g", cMax, math.Sqrt(3)/2)
	}
	if p := Params[0].C; float64(p) >= cMax {
		t.Errorf("Params.C default %g is at or above the CFL limit %g", p, cMax)
	}
}
GOEOF

## One thing you need to know: the CFL limit tightened

```
TestLaplacian26CFL  lambda_min = -5.333333 (want -16/3, attained at k=(pi,pi,0))
                    CFL limit: C < 0.866025 (sqrt(3)/2)
```

The isotropic weights have spectral radius **16/3** instead of 4, so the stability bound drops from $C < 1$ to $C < \sqrt3/2 = 0.8660$. **Isotropy costs about 13% of the timestep.** That's a real trade, not a free win — worth knowing if you ever push `C` up. Your default of 0.5 is unaffected, and the test asserts it stays under the limit.

I've updated the `Params.C` doc comment, which said "generally should not exceed 1" — that guidance was exactly right for the old weights and is now wrong by 13%.

The electroweak tests are unaffected because they're all $k=0$, where both stencils return exactly zero regardless of weighting.

  # Paper Summary
  
  **Title:** Isotropic discrete Laplacian operators from lattice hydrodynamics
  
  **Authors:** Sumesh P. Thampi, Santosh Ansumali, Ronojoy Adhikari, Sauro Succi
  
  **Year:** 2012
  
  **Journal Reference:** Journal of Computational Physics, Vol. 237, pp. 1-7 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2012.07.037)
  
  **Abstract:** The authors demonstrate that "discrete schemes developed for lattice hydrodynamics provide an elegant and physically transparent way of deriving Laplacians with isotropic discretisation error." They explain that isotropy is guaranteed when Laplacian weights come from the discrete Maxwell-Boltzmann equilibrium, which are inherently isotropic on lattices. A key finding is that "stencils using as few as 15 points in three dimensions, generate isotropic Laplacians," making them computationally efficient alternatives to larger anisotropic stencils. The methodology extends to higher-order discretizations and other differential operators like gradient, divergence, and curl.

  Numerical Anisotropy in Finite Differencing
  Adrian Sescu∗
  
  arXiv:1902.04466v1 [math.NA] 12 Feb 2019
  
  Department of Aerospace Engineering, Mississippi State University, MS 39762
  
  Abstract
  Numerical solutions to hyperbolic partial differential equations, involving wave propagations
  in one direction, are subject to several specific errors, such as numerical dispersion, dissipation or
  aliasing. In multi-dimensions, where the waves propagate in all directions, there is an additional
  specific error resulting from the discretization of spatial derivatives along grid lines. Specifically, waves or wave packets in multi-dimensions propagate at different phase or group velocities,
  respectively, along different directions. A commonly used term for the aforementioned multidimensional discretization error is the numerical anisotropy or isotropy error. In this review, the
  numerical anisotropy is briefly described in the context of the wave equation in multi-dimensions.
  Then, several important studies that were focused on optimizations of finite difference schemes
  with the objective of reducing the numerical anisotropy are discussed.

import numpy as np, itertools, math
offs=[np.array(o,dtype=float) for o in itertools.product((-1,0,1),repeat=3) if any(o)]
ks=np.linspace(0,np.pi,61)
def wt(t): return np.array([t[int(o@o)] for o in offs])
def iso(w):
    q4=sum(x*o[0]**4 for x,o in zip(w,offs)); q22=sum(x*o[0]**2*o[1]**2 for x,o in zip(w,offs))
    n=sum(x*o[0]**2 for x,o in zip(w,offs)); return n, 3*q22/q4
def lmin(w):
    m=0.0
    for a in ks:
        for b in ks:
            for c in ks:
                k=np.array([a,b,c]); m=min(m,sum(x*(math.cos(k@o)-1.0) for x,o in zip(w,offs)))
    return m
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); dirs=[d/np.linalg.norm(d) for d in rng.standard_normal((1500,3))]
def spread(w,km):
    r=[(-sum(x*(math.cos((km*d)@o)-1.0) for x,o in zip(w,offs)))/(km*km) for d in dirs]
    return 100*(max(r)-min(r))

rows=[("7-pt (faces only)",   {0:0,1:1/3,2:0,3:0}),
      ("19-pt 1/d^2  (Barkley/OB)",{0:0,1:1/3,2:1/6,3:0}),
      ("27-pt 1/d^2  (OB 2006)", {0:0,1:3/13,2:3/26,3:1/13}),
      ("27-pt 14:3:1 (Mehrstellen)",{0:0,1:14/30,2:3/30,3:1/30}),
      ("27-pt 28:10:1 (ours)",  {0:0,1:28/72,2:10/72,3:1/72})]
print(f"{'stencil':28} {'norm':>6} {'iso ratio':>10} {'lam_min':>9} {'dt diff':>8} {'C wave':>8} {'spread@0.8':>11}")

import numpy as np, itertools, math
offs=[np.array(o,dtype=float) for o in itertools.product((-1,0,1),repeat=3) if any(o)]
def wt(t): return np.array([t[int(o@o)] for o in offs])
a=wt({0:0,1:1/3,2:1/6,3:0})          # 19-point (c3=0)
b=wt({0:0,1:28/72,2:10/72,3:1/72})   # our 27-point isotropic
ks=np.linspace(0,np.pi,41); worst=0.0; wk=None
for x in ks:
    for y in ks:
        for z in ks:
            k=np.array([x,y,z])
            la=sum(w*(math.cos(k@o)-1) for w,o in zip(a,offs))
            lb=sum(w*(math.cos(k@o)-1) for w,o in zip(b,offs))
            if abs(la-lb)>worst: worst, wk = abs(la-lb), k
print(f"max |symbol difference| over the Brillouin zone = {worst:.6f}  at k={wk}")
print(f"  (for scale, |lambda_min| = 16/3 = {16/3:.4f}, so that is {100*worst/(16/3):.2f}% of full scale)")

I searched, and **I could not find one** — and I think the evidence is stronger than a mere negative result.

## Why the reviewer was probably wrong

[Thampi, Ansumali, Adhikari & Succi (2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.3299), *J. Comput. Phys.* 237, 1–7, "Isotropic discrete Laplacian operators from lattice hydrodynamics" is a peer-reviewed JCP paper on exactly this topic. Its literature review says:

> "Two recent studies have addressed this issue, by providing algebraic methods for constructing isotropic Laplacians [1, 2]."

Refs [1] and [2] are **Kumar, JCP 201 (2004) 109** and **Patra & Karttunen, Numer. Meth. PDE 22 (2006) 936**. That's it. And they add that lattice-Boltzmann weights have been known a long time "but their connection to isotropic Laplacians has not been recognized" — i.e. as of 2012, in a paper by Succi, who wrote the standard LB textbook, this was still treated as new ground.

Likewise [Sescu's 2019 review](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.04466) of numerical anisotropy in finite differencing has 48 references and nothing earlier than Yee (1966) and Trefethen (1982) on the anisotropy question.

If a 1950s Soviet paper had settled this, those two communities would cite it.

## What prior art does exist (and would have been the honest review)

- **Mikeladze (1938)**, *Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat.*, 271–292 — on the numerical solution of Laplace/Poisson by difference schemes. This is the closest thing to "a Russian, mid-century," and it's routinely cited as the origin of high-order **compact** schemes. But it's about order of accuracy, not stencil isotropy or timestep.
- **The Mehrstellen 27-point stencil**, weights **14 : 3 : 1** (face:edge:corner, over 30) — a [known compact scheme](https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1844490), Collatz's textbook being the standard reference. The stencil *geometry* and one specific weighting long predate 2006. But Mehrstellen optimizes accuracy by also averaging the right-hand side; it isn't a large-stencil explicit scheme chosen for timestep.
- **Shinozaki & Oono (1993)**, *Phys. Rev. E* 48, 2622 — used an isotropic 27-point Laplacian for 3D phase separation.
- **Qian, d'Humières & Lallemand (1992)**, *EPL* 17, 479 — the D3Q27 weights.
- **Dowle, Mantel & Barkley (1997)** — the 19-point, which you do cite.

## The likely proximate cause

Your paper has **exactly one reference**. A numerical-analysis submission with a single citation is going to draw "surely someone did this before" almost regardless of content — and a reviewer who can't name the source is often reacting to that, not to actual knowledge. With Collatz/Mehrstellen, Barkley, and the LB weights positioned as related-but-different, the same result would have read as a contribution rather than a rediscovery.

## The part that's actually new — and you were right

Running the isotropy condition $\sum w\,\delta_x^4 = 3\sum w\,\delta_x^2\delta_y^2$ on your own stencils:

```
stencil                        norm  iso ratio   lam_min  dt diff   C wave  spread@0.8
7-pt (faces only)             0.667     0.0000   -4.0000   0.5000   1.0000     1.1488%
19-pt 1/d^2  (Barkley/OB)     2.000     1.0000   -5.3333   0.3750   0.8660     0.0545%
27-pt 1/d^2  (OB 2006)        2.000     1.6154   -4.0000   0.5000   1.0000     1.9710%
27-pt 14:3:1 (Mehrstellen)    2.000     1.0000   -6.1333   0.3261   0.8076     0.0723%
27-pt 28:10:1 (ours)          2.000     1.0000   -5.3333   0.3750   0.8660     0.0545%
```

**Your 19-point $1/d^2$ stencil is exactly isotropic** — ratio 1.0000, not approximately. It sits precisely on the condition, as the $c_3 = 0$ member of the family. Your conclusion said *"For maximum rotational symmetry, the 19-point stencil appears to be the best"* — that's provably correct, and it's a sharper statement than the paper makes. Extending $1/d^2$ out to the corners is exactly what breaks it.

And your $\Delta t$ numbers fall straight out: $2/|\lambda_{\min}|$ gives 0.375 for the 19-point and 0.5 for the 27-point, matching the abstract. So the trade-off you found empirically is real and now has a closed form: **the 27-point $1/d^2$ buys 33% more timestep by giving up isotropy; the 19-point is the isotropic optimum.** That's a Pareto front, not an error — you were optimizing timestep, and $1/d^2$ is optimal for that.

Notably, Mehrstellen's 14:3:1 is isotropic but *worse than yours on both axes*.

## One implication for the code

All isotropic members with $c_3 \lesssim 1/48$ have identical $\lambda_{\min}$ and identical directional spread — adding corners buys nothing. So the 28:10:1 I put in is numerically equivalent to your 19-point at low $k$ (they differ 16.7% only at the checkerboard mode $k = (\pi,\pi,\pi)$). If you'd rather use the 19-point weighting, it's the same isotropy and the same CFL with **8 fewer neighbor reads per site** — a real GPU win if you restructure `NeighOffs` to skip corners. Say the word and I'll do it.

		FaceOffs[dim, Minus1, j, math32.X] = mx
		FaceOffs[dim, Minus1, j, math32.Y] = my
		FaceOffs[dim, Minus1, j, math32.Z] = mz
		FaceOffs[dim, Plus1, j, math32.X] = -mx
		FaceOffs[dim, Plus1, j, math32.Y] = -my
		FaceOffs[dim, Plus1, j, math32.Z] = -mz

		setPair(math32.Y, int32(j), a, -1, b)
		setPair(math32.Z, int32(j), a, b, -1)
	}

// --- Curl18 / Divergence18 -------------------------------------------------

// stFill3 writes a vector field into three CONSECUTIVE state variables
// starting at v, which is the layout Curl18 and Divergence18 expect.
func stFill3(v int32, f func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64) {
	n := stSize + 2
	for z := range n {
		for y := range n {
			for x := range n {
				a := f(float64(x-stCtr), float64(y-stCtr), float64(z-stCtr))
				for c := range 3 {
					State.Set(float32(a[c]), z, y, x, int(v)+c, 0)
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

// TestCurl18 checks the curl on fields whose answer is known exactly.
// Curl18 is built entirely from Grad18Wts and FaceOffs, so it inherits the
// gradient's normalization and isotropy; what needs checking here is that the
// six directional derivatives are paired into the right antisymmetric
// combinations, and with the right signs.
func TestCurl18(t *testing.T) {
	stencilSim()
	v := int32(EWHsCa)
	c := int32(stCtr)

	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name string
		f    func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64
		want [3]float64
	}{
		{"constant", func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64 { return [3]float64{2, -3, 5} },
			[3]float64{0, 0, 0}},
		{"rigid rotation (-y,x,0)", func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64 { return [3]float64{-y, x, 0} },
			[3]float64{0, 0, 2}},
		{"(0,0,y)", func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64 { return [3]float64{0, 0, y} },
			[3]float64{1, 0, 0}},
		{"(z,0,0)", func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64 { return [3]float64{z, 0, 0} },
			[3]float64{0, 1, 0}},
		// curl of a gradient vanishes identically; a quadratic potential makes
		// the gradient field linear, so this is exact rather than asymptotic
		{"grad(x^2+2yz)", func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64 {
			return [3]float64{2 * x, 2 * z, 2 * y}
		}, [3]float64{0, 0, 0}},
	} {
		stFill3(v, tc.f)
		g := Curl18(c, c, c, v, 0)
		got := [3]float64{float64(g.X), float64(g.Y), float64(g.Z)}
		for i := range 3 {
			if math.Abs(got[i]-tc.want[i]) > 1e-5 {
				t.Errorf("curl(%s) = %v, want %v", tc.name, got, tc.want)
				break
			}
		}
	}

	// a general linear field A_i = M_ij r_j has curl_i = eps_ijk M_kj exactly
	rng := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(7, 8))
	worst := 0.0
	for range 50 {
		var m [3][3]float64
		for i := range 3 {
			for j := range 3 {
				m[i][j] = rng.NormFloat64()
			}
		}
		stFill3(v, func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64 {
			r := [3]float64{x, y, z}
			var a [3]float64
			for i := range 3 {
				for j := range 3 {
					a[i] += m[i][j] * r[j]
				}
			}
			return a
		})
		g := Curl18(c, c, c, v, 0)
		want := [3]float64{m[2][1] - m[1][2], m[0][2] - m[2][0], m[1][0] - m[0][1]}
		got := [3]float64{float64(g.X), float64(g.Y), float64(g.Z)}
		for i := range 3 {
			worst = math.Max(worst, math.Abs(got[i]-want[i]))
		}
	}
	t.Logf("curl of 50 random linear vector fields: max error %.3e", worst)
	if worst > 1e-5 {
		t.Errorf("curl not exact on linear fields: max error %g", worst)
	}
}

// TestDivergence18 checks div on linear fields, where it equals trace(M).
// It also checks the per-direction out-params, which the previous version of
// the function never wrote.
func TestDivergence18(t *testing.T) {
	stencilSim()
	v := int32(EWHsCa)
	c := int32(stCtr)
	rng := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(9, 10))
	worst, worstC := 0.0, 0.0
	for range 50 {
		var m [3][3]float64
		for i := range 3 {
			for j := range 3 {
				m[i][j] = rng.NormFloat64()
			}
		}
		stFill3(v, func(x, y, z float64) [3]float64 {
			r := [3]float64{x, y, z}
			var a [3]float64
			for i := range 3 {
				for j := range 3 {
					a[i] += m[i][j] * r[j]
				}
			}
			return a
		})
		var dx, dy, dz float32
		got := float64(Divergence18(c, c, c, v, 0, &dx, &dy, &dz))
		want := m[0][0] + m[1][1] + m[2][2]
		worst = math.Max(worst, math.Abs(got-want))
		// the out-params are the diagonal terms d_i A_i individually
		for i, d := range []float32{dx, dy, dz} {
			worstC = math.Max(worstC, math.Abs(float64(d)-m[i][i]))
		}
	}
	t.Logf("divergence of 50 random linear fields: max error %.3e (components %.3e)", worst, worstC)
	if worst > 1e-5 || worstC > 1e-5 {
		t.Errorf("divergence not exact on linear fields: %g (components %g)", worst, worstC)
	}
}
GOEOF

All 13 pass. Here's what changed.

## Both stencils now drop the corners

| operator | weights | points read | vs before |
|---|---|---|---|
| Laplacian | 2 : 1 : 0 | **18** (was 26) | 31% fewer |
| Gradient / Curl / Divergence | 2 : 1 : 0 | **10** (was 18) | 44% fewer |

`NeighOffs` and `FaceOffs` are now ordered **by shell** (faces, edges, corners), which is what lets the loops stop early rather than multiplying by zero. Three named constants in the gosl section carry the intent: `NNeigh = 26`, `NLapNeigh = 18`, `NGradPair = 5`. `NeighAverage27` and `NeighMax26` still use all 26, since they genuinely need them.

The gradient came out **cheaper *and* more isotropic** than the 16:4:1 I had:

```
|k|=0.3  Laplacian26 spread 0.0011%   Gradient18 spread 0.0033%   (was 0.0040%)
|k|=0.8  Laplacian26 spread 0.0546%   Gradient18 spread 0.1615%   (was 0.1903%)
```

CFL is unchanged at $C < \sqrt3/2$ — the 19-point and the 27-point isotropic weights have the same spectral radius, which is exactly why the corners were never earning their keep.

## Curl18: tested, and it was fine

It's built entirely from `Grad18Wts` and `FaceOffs`, so it inherits the normalization and isotropy automatically — fixing the gradient fixed it. What needed independent checking was whether the six directional derivatives are paired into the right antisymmetric combinations with the right signs. They are:

```
curl of 50 random linear vector fields: max error 2.949e-07
```

plus exact cases: constant field → 0, rigid rotation $(-y,x,0)$ → $(0,0,2)$, $(0,0,y)$ → $(1,0,0)$, $(z,0,0)$ → $(0,1,0)$, and $\nabla\times\nabla f = 0$ for a quadratic potential.

## Divergence18 was broken

Since I was in there — it used `vidx` for all three directions instead of `vidx+xyz`, so it computed $\partial_x A + \partial_y A + \partial_z A$ of a **single scalar**, not $\nabla\!\cdot\!\vec{A}$. And its `dx, dy, dz` out-params were never written at all. It's never called anywhere, so it was dead WIP code rather than a live bug — but it would have bitten whoever reached for it first. Fixed and tested:

```
divergence of 50 random linear fields: max error 3.431e-07 (components 2.621e-07)
```

The out-params now carry the individual $\partial_i A_i$ terms, which seems the likeliest reason they were there.

## One loose end: the names are now stale

`Laplacian26` reads 18 neighbors; `Gradient18` and `Curl18` read 10 points. That's a trap for whoever reads this next. I left them alone because renaming touches ~38 call sites across eight kernel files plus regenerated WGSL, and I'd rather that be its own commit than buried in a numerics change — but the doc comments now state the actual counts prominently. Say the word and I'll do the rename (`Laplacian19`, `Gradient10`, `Curl10`, `Divergence10`, matching your paper's convention) as a clean mechanical pass.

## Where the stencil work landed

Four things came out of this thread, worth keeping straight:

1. **Both stencils were anisotropic** — the $1/d^2$ and $1/d$ weightings normalize correctly but miss the isotropy conditions by 1.615× and 1.82×. Now exactly 1.000 on both.
2. **Your 19-point was already exactly isotropic** — extending $1/d^2$ to the corners is what broke it, and your paper's conclusion said so without proof. The corners are now skipped: 31% fewer reads for the Laplacian, 44% for the gradient family.
3. **`Divergence10` was broken** — differentiated one scalar in three directions instead of three components, and never wrote its out-params. Dead code, now fixed and tested.
4. **CFL tightened** to $C < \sqrt3/2$, documented on `Params.C`, with a test that pins the spectral radius at exactly $-16/3$ and checks the default stays under it.

The one thing I'd still flag: this changes numerical output in *every* kernel, so any saved reference results predating today will differ. The electroweak tests are immune only because they're all $k=0$.

Yang–Mills self-coupling is still the open item on the electroweak side whenever you want it.

Now the kernel. Writing the Yang–Mills terms as adjoint-space cross products:

<details>

- **Bash**: `Ran `cd /Users/oreilly/wavereality/waves/wavesim && python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p="electroweak.goal"; s=open(p).read()

helpers = r'''// EWCrossUp returns sum_mu (A^mu x B_mu), the contraction of an UPPER with a
// LOWER spacetime index. No metric signs: all four terms add.
//
// Every eps^{abc} in the Yang-Mills equation is a cross product in adjoint
// space, since eps^{abc} X^b Y^c = (X x Y)^a. Writing the self-coupling this
// way turns a triple-index mess into four cross products.
func EWCrossUp(a0, ax, ay, az, b0, bx, by, bz math32.Vector3) math32.Vector3 {
	r := slmath.Cross3(a0, b0)
	r = r.Add(slmath.Cross3(ax, bx))
	r = r.Add(slmath.Cross3(ay, by))
	r = r.Add(slmath.Cross3(az, bz))
	return r
}

// EWCrossLor returns sum_mu (A_mu x B^mu) where BOTH carry the same index
// position, so the (+,-,-,-) metric appears: time adds, space subtracts.
func EWCrossLor(a0, ax, ay, az, b0, bx, by, bz math32.Vector3) math32.Vector3 {
	r := slmath.Cross3(a0, b0)
	r = r.Sub(slmath.Cross3(ax, bx))
	r = r.Sub(slmath.Cross3(ay, by))
	r = r.Sub(slmath.Cross3(az, bz))
	return r
}

'''
s = s.replace("// ElectroweakKernel is the kernel for the SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y electroweak model:",

<details>
<summary>Tool Calls (1)</summary>

- **Bash**: `Ran `cd /Users/oreilly/wavereality/waves/wavesim && rm -f dbg_test.go sz_test.go && cat >> electroweak_test.go <<'GOEOF'

// --- Yang-Mills self-coupling ---------------------------------------------

// ymSim is pure Yang-Mills: HiggsMu = 0 makes vfac = -lambda*mag, so Phi = 0
// is an exact fixed point and every Higgs current vanishes identically. What
// is left is the gauge sector alone.
func ymSim(sz int32) *Sim {
	ss := ewSim(sz)
	ss.Params.HiggsMu = 0
	ss.Params.Update()
	State.SetZeros()
	GetCtx(0).Init()
	return ss
}

// ewWBase returns the first state variable of SU(2) component a (1..3);
// the four potentials are at +0..+3 and their velocities at +4..+7.
func ewWBase(a int) int { return int(EWW10s) + (a-1)*8 }

// TestYangMillsPureGauge is the acceptance test for the self-coupling.
//
// A constant uniform W^3_0 = B over a vacuum gauge field is PURE GAUGE: it is
// the gauge transform, by U = exp(i g B c t T^3), of a static uniform W^1_x.
// So the exact solution has (W^1_x, W^2_x) turning in the adjoint 1-2 plane at
//
//	omega = -c * g * B
//
// with |W| constant and W^3_0 standing still. Consistency of BOTH the nu = x
// and the nu = 0 equations is needed for that, and they involve different
// terms, which is what makes this test pin down all the coefficients at once:
//
//	nu = x: transport (-2g) and quartic (-g^2) must cancel to leave -omega^2 W
//	nu = 0: transpose (+g) and quartic (-g^2) must cancel exactly
//
// Get the factor of 2 on transport wrong, or the sign of the transpose term,
// and the radius runs away instead of holding. Reversing the rotation sense
// makes the rate wrong by 2x and W^3_0 collapse, so the sign is discriminated
// too.
//
// As in TestGaugeTimeComponent the rotating-frame system is only marginally
// stable under an explicit integrator, so the radius error is measured as a
// convergence rate rather than an absolute.
func TestYangMillsPureGauge(t *testing.T) {
	const drSteps = 64
	var prevDrift float64
	var ratios []float64
	r := float32(0.05)
	t.Logf("%8s %11s %12s %9s %13s %8s %12s", "B", "omega", "measured", "ratio", "drift/step", "x4?", "W30 drift")
	for k, b := range []float32{0.02, 0.01, 0.005} {
		ss := ymSim(4)
		p := ss.Params
		om := -float64(p.C) * float64(p.GW) * float64(b)
		ss.Fill(EWW30s, Both, b)
		ss.Fill(EWW1Xs, Both, r)
		ss.Fill(EWW2Xv, Both, float32(om)*r)
		ewWrap()

		n1 := int(0.4 / math.Abs(om))
		nrun := 2 * n1
		if nrun < drSteps {
			nrun = drSteps
		}
		r0 := float64(r) * float64(r)
		var th1, th2, drift float64
		for i := range nrun {
			ewStep(ss)
			switch i + 1 {
			case n1:
				th1 = math.Atan2(float64(ewGet(EWW2Xs)), float64(ewGet(EWW1Xs)))
			case 2 * n1:
				th2 = math.Atan2(float64(ewGet(EWW2Xs)), float64(ewGet(EWW1Xs)))
			case drSteps:
				w1, w2 := float64(ewGet(EWW1Xs)), float64(ewGet(EWW2Xs))
				drift = math.Abs((w1*w1+w2*w2)-r0) / (r0 * drSteps)
			}
		}
		got := (th2 - th1) / float64(n1)
		bd := math.Abs(float64(ewGet(EWW30s)-b)) / float64(b)
		scale := ""
		if k > 0 {
			ratios = append(ratios, prevDrift/drift)
			scale = fmt.Sprintf("%.2f", prevDrift/drift)
		}
		prevDrift = drift
		t.Logf("%8.3f %11.6f %12.6f %9.4f %13.3e %8s %11.2e", b, om, got, got/om, drift, scale, bd)

		// tolerance covers the scheme's own O(omega) phase error, as in
		// TestGaugeTimeComponent; the sharp assertion is the drift scaling
		if math.IsNaN(got) || math.Abs(got/om-1) > 0.02 {
			t.Errorf("B=%g: rotation %g, want -c*g*B = %g", b, got, om)
		}
		if bd > 0.02 {
			t.Errorf("B=%g: W^3_0 drifted %.3g relative; pure gauge must hold it", b, bd)
		}
	}
	for i, rr := range ratios {
		if math.IsNaN(rr) || math.Abs(rr-4.0) > 0.6 {
			t.Errorf("step %d: radius drift scaled by %.3f when omega halved, want ~4", i, rr)
		}
	}
}

// TestYangMillsCovariance checks the eps^{abc} structure with NON-uniform
// fields, which the pure-gauge test cannot reach.
//
// A constant SO(3) rotation of the adjoint index is an exact symmetry of the
// Yang-Mills equations, because eps is invariant under SO(3) and the Laplacian
// and gradients act componentwise. So rotating the initial condition, evolving,
// and rotating back must reproduce plain evolution. Using a signed permutation
// (90 degrees about the 3-axis: W1 -> -W2, W2 -> W1) makes the comparison exact
// in floating point rather than merely close.
func TestYangMillsCovariance(t *testing.T) {
	const sz, nst = 6, 40
	fill := func(ss *Sim) {
		n := int(sz) + 2
		for z := range n {
			for y := range n {
				for x := range n {
					for a := 1; a <= 3; a++ {
						for c := range 4 {
							v := 0.03 * math.Sin(float64(a+c)+0.7*float64(x)+
								0.5*float64(y)-0.3*float64(z))
							State.Set(float32(v), z, y, x, ewWBase(a)+c, 0)
							State.Set(float32(v), z, y, x, ewWBase(a)+c, 1)
						}
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}
	// rotate 90 degrees about adjoint axis 3: (W1, W2, W3) -> (-W2, W1, W3)
	rot := func(inv bool) {
		n := int(sz) + 2
		s := 1.0
		if inv {
			s = -1.0
		}
		for z := range n {
			for y := range n {
				for x := range n {
					for c := range 8 {
						w1 := State.Value(z, y, x, ewWBase(1)+c, 0)
						w2 := State.Value(z, y, x, ewWBase(2)+c, 0)
						State.Set(float32(-s)*w2, z, y, x, ewWBase(1)+c, 0)
						State.Set(float32(s)*w1, z, y, x, ewWBase(2)+c, 0)
						for tt := range 2 {
							_ = tt
						}
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}
	// plain evolution
	ss := ymSim(sz)
	fill(ss)
	ewWrap()
	for range nst {
		ewStep(ss)
	}
	plain := make([]float32, 0, 4096)
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	n := int(sz) + 2
	for z := range n {
		for y := range n {
			for x := range n {
				for a := 1; a <= 3; a++ {
					for c := range 8 {
						plain = append(plain, State.Value(z, y, x, ewWBase(a)+c, cur))
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}

	// rotate -> evolve -> rotate back
	ss2 := ymSim(sz)
	fill(ss2)
	rot(false)
	ewWrap()
	for range nst {
		ewStep(ss2)
	}
	// bring the result back into the cur slot layout rot() edits
	cur2 := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	worst := 0.0
	i := 0
	for z := range n {
		for y := range n {
			for x := range n {
				for c := range 8 {
					w1 := State.Value(z, y, x, ewWBase(1)+c, cur2)
					w2 := State.Value(z, y, x, ewWBase(2)+c, cur2)
					// inverse rotation: (W1,W2) -> (W2,-W1)
					got := []float32{w2, -w1, State.Value(z, y, x, ewWBase(3)+c, cur2)}
					for a := range 3 {
						worst = math.Max(worst, math.Abs(float64(got[a]-plain[i+a*8+c])))
					}
				}
				i += 24
			}
		}
	}
	t.Logf("global SO(3) covariance over %d steps on a %d^3 lattice: max deviation %.3e", nst, sz, worst)
	if worst > 1e-6 {
		t.Errorf("Yang-Mills not covariant under a constant adjoint rotation: %g", worst)
	}
}
GOEOF

// self-coupling: every term is quadratic or cubic in W, so all four vanish at
// linear order and cannot shift a boson mass. Turning them on must leave the
// W frequency alone, up to the O(eps^2) correction they genuinely do produce.
func TestYangMillsSpectrumUnchanged(t *testing.T) {
	eps := float32(1e-4)
	nsteps := 3000
	var freq [2]float64
	for i, on := range []bool{false, true} {

		ss.Params.YangMills.SetBool(on)

		ss.Fill(EWW1Xs, Both, eps)

		freq[i] = freqZC(y)
	}
	rel := math.Abs(freq[1]/freq[0] - 1)
	t.Logf("W frequency: YangMills off %.8f, on %.8f -- relative shift %.2e (kick eps = %.0e)",
		freq[0], freq[1], rel, eps)
	if rel > 1e-5 {
		t.Errorf("Yang-Mills terms shifted the W mass by %g; they must vanish at linear order", rel)

}

## The implementation

The key simplification: **every $\varepsilon^{abc}$ is a cross product in adjoint space**, since $\varepsilon^{abc}X^bY^c = (\vec X \times \vec Y)^a$. Grouping the $W^a$ into adjoint 3-vectors $\vec{W}_\mu = (W^1_\mu, W^2_\mu, W^3_\mu)$ turns a triple-index mess into two helpers and a handful of `slmath.Cross3` calls:

$$\Box W^a_\nu = j^a_\nu \underbrace{- g\,\varepsilon^{abc}(\partial\!\cdot\!W^b)W^c_\nu}_{\text{divergence}} \underbrace{- 2g\,\varepsilon^{abc}W^{b\mu}\partial_\mu W^c_\nu}_{\text{transport}} \underbrace{+ g\,\varepsilon^{abc}W^b_\mu\partial^\nu W^{c\mu}}_{\text{transpose}} \underbrace{- g^2\varepsilon^{abc}\varepsilon^{cde}(W^b\!\cdot\!W^d)W^e_\nu}_{\text{quartic}}$$

`EWCrossUp` handles upper–lower contractions (no metric signs), `EWCrossLor` handles same-position ones (time adds, space subtracts). Gated by `Params.YangMills`.

Two things worth flagging about the derivation:

- **The divergence term is kept, not dropped.** Unlike the abelian case, $\partial\!\cdot\!W^a = 0$ is *not* preserved by non-abelian evolution, so it can't simply be imposed. I used a Feynman-type gauge-fixing term ($\xi=1$) to cancel the $-\partial^\nu(\partial\!\cdot\!W)$ piece instead.
- **Transport and transpose use transposes of the same tensor** — $\partial_\mu W^\nu$ versus $\partial^\nu W^\mu$. I had them swapped on first write and caught it on review before testing; worth knowing since they'd be easy to conflate again.

The 12 `Gradient10` calls pull double duty: their traces give the divergences the Higgs covariant Laplacian already needed, so `EWDiv` for the three W fields is now free.

## Tests

**`TestYangMillsPureGauge`** is the acceptance test. A uniform $W^3_0 = B$ is the gauge transform of a static $W^1_x$, so $(W^1_x, W^2_x)$ must turn at $\omega = -cgB$ with $|W|$ held and $W^3_0$ still. Crucially, consistency of *both* the $\nu=x$ and $\nu=0$ equations is required, and they involve different terms — so one test pins every coefficient:

```
       B       omega     measured     ratio    drift/step      x4?    W30 drift
   0.020   -0.006533    -0.006569    1.0055     4.261e-05             3.42e-03
   0.010   -0.003266    -0.003283    1.0051     1.067e-05     3.99    6.80e-03
   0.005   -0.001633    -0.001645    1.0073     2.667e-06     4.00    1.34e-02
```

Radius drift converges as $O(\omega^2)$ — the integrator, not the physics. The sign is discriminated hard: running $\omega = +cgB$ instead gives rate ratios of 2.15 and −6.55, drift three orders larger that doesn't scale, and $W^3_0$ collapsing from +0.01 to −0.15.

**`TestYangMillsCovariance`** reaches what the pure-gauge test can't — non-uniform fields. A constant SO(3) rotation of the adjoint index is an exact symmetry, so rotate → evolve → unrotate must reproduce plain evolution. Using a 90° signed permutation makes it exact in floating point: **max deviation 2.98e−8**, the float32 floor, over 40 steps on $6^3$.

**`TestYangMillsSpectrumUnchanged`** confirms the defining property — all four terms vanish at linear order:

```
W frequency: YangMills off 0.02008916, on 0.02008916 -- relative shift 0.00e+00
```

## What's still not pinned

Covariance is blind to an overall scale on the whole self-coupling, and the pure-gauge test exercises the terms in specific combinations rather than individually. A YM energy functional with a conservation check would close that gap completely — that's the natural next hardening step if you want it.

Also unchanged: the rotating-frame instability applies here too. Sustained large $W_0$ over many periods will run away under symplectic Euler, for the same reason as the $\mathcal{G}_0$ sector. A Boris-style push would fix both at once.

The mismatch is $O(k^2)$, i.e. $O(a^2)$ — a discretization artifact, not an error. So the right test is a **convergence** statement: force must equal $-\partial U/\partial\phi$ in the continuum limit. A wrong YM coefficient gives an $O(1)$ mismatch that never converges. Writing the static energy:

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import "cogentcore.org/core/math32"

// ElectroweakStaticEnergy is the potential (no time derivative) part of the
// electroweak energy, evaluated over the interior of the lattice:
//
//	U = sum_x [ (1/2) sum_j |D_j Psi|^2                     Higgs gradient
//	          + V(mag)                                      Higgs potential
//	          + (1/4) sum_{a,j,k} (F^a_jk)^2                W magnetic
//	          + (1/4) sum_{j,k} (Fb_jk)^2                   B magnetic
//	          + (1/2) sum_a (div W^a)^2 + (1/2)(div B)^2 ]  gauge fixing
//
// with the full non-abelian field strength
//
//	F^a_jk = d_j W^a_k - d_k W^a_j + g eps^abc W^b_j W^c_k
//
// The gauge-fixing term is the xi = 1 (Feynman) choice that the kernel's
// equations of motion assume; together with the magnetic term it is what makes
// the abelian part of -dU/dW come out as the plain Laplacian.
//
// This is a host-side diagnostic, used by the tests to check that the kernel's
// force really is -dU/dphi. It is NOT exact at finite lattice spacing, because
// Laplacian19 and Gradient10 are not adjoint-compatible (their Fourier symbols
// differ by O(k^2)); the agreement is a continuum-limit statement, which is
// what TestElectroweakForceIsEnergyGradient measures.
//
// Only W_0 = B_0 = 0 configurations are covered: with a time component present
// the conserved functional is the indefinite Feynman-gauge one, whose cubic
// term mixes kinetic and potential pieces.
func ElectroweakStaticEnergy() float64 {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	p := &Params[0]
	sz := ctx.Size.V()
	g := p.GW
	tot := 0.0
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz.Z; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz.Y; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz.X; x++ {
				tot += float64(ewSiteEnergy(x, y, z, g, p))
			}
		}
	}
	return tot
}

// ewWVec returns the adjoint triplet (W^1_c, W^2_c, W^3_c) for spatial
// component c (0=X, 1=Y, 2=Z) at one site.
func ewWVec(x, y, z, c int32, tidx int32) math32.Vector3 {
	return math32.Vec3(
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWW1Xs)+int(c), int(tidx)),
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWW2Xs)+int(c), int(tidx)),
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWW3Xs)+int(c), int(tidx)))
}

func ewSiteEnergy(x, y, z int32, g float32, p *Parameters) float32 {
	prv := int32(0) // the tests evaluate energy on slice 0
	psi := math32.Vec4(
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWHsCa), 0),
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWHsCb), 0),
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWHs0a), 0),
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWHs0b), 0))

	// ---- Higgs: covariant gradient + potential ----------------------------
	gCa := Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(EWHsCa), prv)
	gCb := Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(EWHsCb), prv)
	g0a := Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(EWHs0a), prv)
	g0b := Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(EWHs0b), prv)
	e := float32(0)
	for c := int32(0); c < 3; c++ {
		var d math32.Vector4
		switch c {
		case 0:
			d = math32.Vec4(gCa.X, gCb.X, g0a.X, g0b.X)
		case 1:
			d = math32.Vec4(gCa.Y, gCb.Y, g0a.Y, g0b.Y)
		default:
			d = math32.Vec4(gCa.Z, gCb.Z, g0a.Z, g0b.Z)
		}
		w := ewWVec(x, y, z, c, prv)
		b := State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWBXs)+int(c), 0)
		d = d.Add(EWGaugeAct(w.X, w.Y, w.Z, b, psi))
		e += 0.5 * (d.X*d.X + d.Y*d.Y + d.Z*d.Z + d.W*d.W)
	}
	mag := psi.X*psi.X + psi.Y*psi.Y + psi.Z*psi.Z + psi.W*psi.W
	e += -0.5*p.HiggsMuSq*mag + 0.25*p.HiggsLambda*mag*mag

	// ---- gauge field strengths -------------------------------------------
	// gradients of the three spatial components of each field
	var gw [3]math32.Vector3 // gw[c] = grad of W^?_c -- per adjoint below
	_ = gw
	var gW [3][3]math32.Vector3 // [adjoint a][component c]
	for a := 0; a < 3; a++ {
		for c := 0; c < 3; c++ {
			gW[a][c] = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(EWW1Xs)+int32(a*8+c), prv)
		}
	}
	var gB [3]math32.Vector3
	for c := 0; c < 3; c++ {
		gB[c] = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(EWBXs)+int32(c), prv)
	}
	comp := func(v math32.Vector3, i int) float32 {
		switch i {
		case 0:
			return v.X
		case 1:
			return v.Y
		}
		return v.Z
	}
	wv := [3]math32.Vector3{ewWVec(x, y, z, 0, prv), ewWVec(x, y, z, 1, prv), ewWVec(x, y, z, 2, prv)}
	bv := [3]float32{
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWBXs), 0),
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWBYs), 0),
		State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWBZs), 0)}

	// magnetic: (1/4) F_jk F_jk, summed over BOTH orderings of (j,k)
	for j := 0; j < 3; j++ {
		for k := 0; k < 3; k++ {
			if j == k {
				continue
			}
			cr := slCross(wv[j], wv[k]) // eps^abc W^b_j W^c_k
			for a := 0; a < 3; a++ {
				f := comp(gW[a][k], j) - comp(gW[a][j], k) + g*comp(cr, a)
				e += 0.25 * f * f
			}
			fb := comp(gB[k], j) - comp(gB[j], k)
			e += 0.25 * fb * fb
		}
	}
	// gauge fixing: (1/2)(div W^a)^2 and (1/2)(div B)^2
	for a := 0; a < 3; a++ {
		dv := gW[a][0].X + gW[a][1].Y + gW[a][2].Z
		e += 0.5 * dv * dv
	}
	dvb := gB[0].X + gB[1].Y + gB[2].Z
	e += 0.5 * dvb * dvb
	return e
}

func slCross(a, b math32.Vector3) math32.Vector3 {
	return math32.Vec3(a.Y*b.Z-a.Z*b.Y, a.Z*b.X-a.X*b.Z, a.X*b.Y-a.Y*b.X)
}

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"
)

// ewFillSmooth lays down a smooth W configuration with wavelength L cubes in
// each direction, with W_0 = B_0 = 0 and all velocities zero. Only the spatial
// gauge components are populated, which is the sector ElectroweakStaticEnergy
// covers.
func ewFillSmooth(sz int32, L float64, amp float32) {
	n := int(sz) + 2
	k := 2 * math.Pi / L
	for z := range n {
		for y := range n {
			for x := range n {
				for a := 0; a < 3; a++ {
					for c := 0; c < 3; c++ {
						v := float64(amp) * math.Sin(k*(float64(x)+0.6*float64(y))+
							0.9*float64(a)+1.7*float64(c)) *
							math.Cos(k*(0.8*float64(z)-0.4*float64(y))+0.3*float64(a))
						for t := range 2 {
							State.Set(float32(v), z, y, x, int(EWW1Xs)+a*8+c, t)
						}
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

// ewKernelForce returns the kernel's acceleration on one state variable at one
// site, divided by c^2 -- i.e. the quantity that must equal -dU/dphi. All
// velocities are zero, so one step leaves exactly the force in the velocity.
func ewKernelForce(ss *Sim, vr EWStates, x, y, z int32) float64 {
	save := State.Clone()
	ewStep(ss)
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	f := State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(vr), cur)
	State.CopyFrom(save)
	GetCtx(0).Init()
	return float64(f) / float64(ss.Params.CSq)
}

// TestElectroweakForceIsEnergyGradient is the check that pins down every
// coefficient of the Yang-Mills self-coupling.
//
// The kernel's force must be -dU/dphi for the static energy U. It cannot be
// exactly so at finite lattice spacing, because Laplacian19 and Gradient10 are
// not adjoint-compatible: their Fourier symbols differ by O(k^2) (2.2% at
// |k| = 0.3, 23% at |k| = 1.0). So this is a CONVERGENCE test -- the mismatch
// must fall as the configuration is made smoother.
//
// That is exactly what discriminates a discretization artifact from a wrong
// coefficient: an error in any Yang-Mills term is O(1) in the field amplitude
// and does NOT shrink with wavelength, while the stencil mismatch does.
func TestElectroweakForceIsEnergyGradient(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 8
	amp := float32(0.02)
	cx, cy, cz := int32(3), int32(4), int32(5)
	h := 1e-4

	t.Logf("%8s %14s %14s %12s", "wavelen", "kernel force", "-dU/dphi", "rel mismatch")
	var prev float64
	var ratios []float64
	for i, L := range []float64{6, 12, 24} {
		ss := ymSim(sz)
		ss.Params.YangMills.SetBool(true)
		ss.Params.Update()
		ewFillSmooth(sz, L, amp)
		ewWrap()

		fk := ewKernelForce(ss, EWW1Xs, cx, cy, cz)

		// numerical gradient of U with respect to W^1_x at that site
		base := State.Value(int(cz), int(cy), int(cx), int(EWW1Xs), 0)
		set := func(v float32) {
			for tt := range 2 {
				State.Set(v, int(cz), int(cy), int(cx), int(EWW1Xs), tt)
			}
			ewWrap()
		}
		set(base + float32(h))
		up := ElectroweakStaticEnergy()
		set(base - float32(h))
		dn := ElectroweakStaticEnergy()
		set(base)
		fn := -(up - dn) / (2 * h)

		rel := math.Abs(fk-fn) / math.Max(math.Abs(fn), 1e-12)
		sc := ""
		if i > 0 {
			ratios = append(ratios, prev/rel)
			sc = ""
		}
		prev = rel
		t.Logf("%8.0f %14.6e %14.6e %12.3e %s", L, fk, fn, rel, sc)
	}
	for i, r := range ratios {
		t.Logf("  mismatch shrank %.2fx when the wavelength doubled (want ~4 for O(a^2))", r)
		if math.IsNaN(r) || r < 2.5 {
			t.Errorf("step %d: mismatch scaled %.3f, not converging -- a coefficient is wrong", i, r)
		}
	}
}

My test had a real flaw: a wavelength of 12 or 24 on an 8-cube wrapped lattice isn't periodic, so the boundary injects garbage. Fix: $-\partial U/\partial\phi(x_0)$ only depends on sites within one cube of $x_0$, so I can sum locally and drop periodicity entirely.

<details>
<summary>Tool Calls (1)</summary>

- **Bash**: `Ran `cd /Users/oreilly/wavereality/waves/wavesim && python3 - <<'PYEOF'

	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	p := &Params[0]
	sz := ctx.Size.V()
	g := p.GW
	tot := 0.0
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz.Z; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz.Y; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz.X; x++ {
				tot += float64(ewSiteEnergy(x, y, z, g, p))
			}
		}

}''','''func ElectroweakStaticEnergy() float64 {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	p := &Params[0]
	sz := ctx.Size.V()
	tot := 0.0
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz.Z; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz.Y; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz.X; x++ {
				tot += float64(ewSiteEnergy(x, y, z, p.GW, p))
			}
		}
	}
	return tot
}

// ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear sums the energy over the 27 sites centred on
// (x,y,z). Every stencil here reaches at most one cube, so the energy at a site
// depends on the field only within +-1 of it: the derivative of the TOTAL
// energy with respect to one site's value therefore lives entirely inside this
// block. Summing locally makes the numerical-gradient check independent of the
// boundary, so the test field does not have to be lattice-periodic.
func ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear(x, y, z int32) float64 {
	p := &Params[0]
	tot := 0.0
	for dz := int32(-1); dz <= 1; dz++ {
		for dy := int32(-1); dy <= 1; dy++ {
			for dx := int32(-1); dx <= 1; dx++ {
				tot += float64(ewSiteEnergy(x+dx, y+dy, z+dz, p.GW, p))
			}
		}
	}
	return tot
}''')
open(p,"w").write(s)

Found it — `ewKernelForce` reads the *position* variable, not the velocity. Position after one step is $W + \text{force}$, which is why it tracked $W$ rather than $\nabla^2 W$.

package wavesim

import ("math"; "testing")

// simple 1D configs: transverse W1x = f(z) exercises only the magnetic term;
// longitudinal W1x = f(x) exercises only the gauge-fixing term. Both must give
// -dU/dW = Laplacian(W).
func TestDbgE(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 10
	cx, cy, cz := int32(5), int32(5), int32(5)
	for _, mode := range []string{"transverse f(z)", "longitudinal f(x)"} {
		for _, L := range []float64{8, 16, 32} {
			ss := ymSim(sz)
			ss.Params.YangMills.SetBool(false)
			ss.Params.Update()
			n := sz + 2
			k := 2 * math.Pi / L
			for z := range n { for y := range n { for x := range n {
				var arg float64
				if mode == "transverse f(z)" { arg = k * float64(z) } else { arg = k * float64(x) }
				v := float32(0.02 * math.Sin(arg))
				for tt := range 2 { State.Set(v, z, y, x, int(EWW1Xs), tt) }
			}}}
			w := State.Value(int(cz), int(cy), int(cx), int(EWW1Xs), 0)
			lap := float64(Laplacian19(cx, cy, cz, int32(EWW1Xs), 0, w))
			base := w
			set := func(v float32) { for tt := range 2 { State.Set(v, int(cz), int(cy), int(cx), int(EWW1Xs), tt) } }
			h := 1e-3
			set(base + float32(h)); up := ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear(cx, cy, cz)
			set(base - float32(h)); dn := ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear(cx, cy, cz)
			set(base)
			fn := -(up - dn) / (2 * h)
			t.Logf("%-18s L=%3.0f  Laplacian19=%+.6e  -dU/dphi=%+.6e  ratio=%.5f", mode, L, lap, fn, fn/lap)
		}
	}
}

All four converge at exactly 4.0×. So the energy is right and single plane waves work — my original test field was a *product* of waves whose two modes partially cancel at the probe site, inflating the relative error. Rewriting with a proper plane wave and amplitude large enough that YM actually dominates:

<details>
<summary>Tool Calls (2)</summary>

- **Bash**: `Ran `cd /Users/oreilly/wavereality/waves/wavesim && rm -f dbg_test.go && python3 - <<'PYEOF'

s = s[:i] + r'''// ewFillWave lays down a single plane wave of wavelength L along a general
// direction, in all nine spatial W components with staggered phases. W_0 and
// B_0 stay zero, as do all velocities -- the sector ElectroweakStaticEnergy
// covers.
//
// It must be ONE plane wave, not a product of two. A product is a superposition
// of modes at |k1+k2| and |k1-k2|, whose force contributions can partly cancel
// at the probe site; the relative mismatch then measures that cancellation
// rather than the discretization, and stops converging.
func ewFillWave(sz int32, L float64, amp float32) {
	n := int(sz) + 2
	k := 2 * math.Pi / L
	d := [3]float64{0.5774, 0.5774, 0.5774}
	for z := range n {
		for y := range n {
			for x := range n {
				arg := k * (d[0]*float64(x) + d[1]*float64(y) + d[2]*float64(z))
				for a := 0; a < 3; a++ {
					for c := 0; c < 3; c++ {
						v := float64(amp) * math.Sin(arg+0.9*float64(a)+1.7*float64(c))
						for t := range 2 {
							State.Set(float32(v), z, y, x, int(EWW1Xs)+a*8+c, t)
						}
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

// ewKernelForce returns the kernel's acceleration on one field at one site,
// divided by c^2 -- the quantity that must equal -dU/dphi. All velocities start
// at zero, so one step leaves exactly the force in the VELOCITY variable (vr
// must be the *v enum, not the *s one: the position after a step is
// W + force, which is a different thing entirely).
func ewKernelForce(ss *Sim, vr EWStates, x, y, z int32) float64 {
	save := State.Clone()
	ewStep(ss)
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	f := State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(vr), cur)
	State.CopyFrom(save)
	GetCtx(0).Init()
	return float64(f) / float64(ss.Params.CSq)
}

// ewGradMismatch returns |kernel force - (-dU/dphi)| / |-dU/dphi| for W^1_x at
// the centre of the lattice, on a plane wave of wavelength L.
func ewGradMismatch(sz int32, L float64, amp float32, ym bool) (float64, float64) {
	cx, cy, cz := sz/2, sz/2, sz/2
	ss := ymSim(sz)
	ss.Params.YangMills.SetBool(ym)
	ss.Params.Update()
	ewFillWave(sz, L, amp)
	fk := ewKernelForce(ss, EWW1Xv, cx, cy, cz)
	base := State.Value(int(cz), int(cy), int(cx), int(EWW1Xs), 0)
	set := func(v float32) {
		for tt := range 2 {
			State.Set(v, int(cz), int(cy), int(cx), int(EWW1Xs), tt)
		}
	}
	const h = 1e-3
	set(base + h)
	up := ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear(cx, cy, cz)
	set(base - h)
	dn := ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear(cx, cy, cz)
	set(base)
	fn := -(up - dn) / (2 * h)
	return math.Abs(fk-fn) / math.Max(math.Abs(fn), 1e-30), fn
}

// TestElectroweakForceIsEnergyGradient is the check that pins down every
// coefficient of the Yang-Mills self-coupling.
//
// The kernel's force must be -dU/dphi for the static energy U. It cannot be
// EXACTLY so at finite lattice spacing, because Laplacian19 and Gradient10 are
// not adjoint-compatible: their Fourier symbols differ by O(k^2) (2.2% at
// |k| = 0.3, 23% at |k| = 1.0). So this is a CONVERGENCE test -- the mismatch
// must fall as O(a^2) when the configuration is made smoother.
//
// That is exactly what separates a discretization artifact from a wrong
// coefficient: an error in any Yang-Mills term is O(1) in the field amplitude
// and does NOT shrink with wavelength, while the stencil mismatch does. The
// amplitude is deliberately large enough that the self-coupling dominates the
// force, so the test is sensitive to it; the control run with the terms
// disabled shows the mismatch then stalls instead of converging.
func TestElectroweakForceIsEnergyGradient(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 10
	amp := float32(0.4)
	Ls := []float64{8, 16, 32}

	for _, ym := range []bool{true, false} {
		var prev float64
		var ratios []float64
		for i, L := range Ls {
			rel, fn := ewGradMismatch(sz, L, amp, ym)
			sc := ""
			if i > 0 {
				ratios = append(ratios, prev/rel)
				sc = fmt.Sprintf("  shrank %.2fx", prev/rel)
			}
			prev = rel
			t.Logf("YangMills=%-5v  L=%3.0f  -dU/dphi=%+.5e  mismatch=%.4e%s", ym, L, fn, rel, sc)
		}
		if ym {
			for i, r := range ratios {
				if math.IsNaN(r) || r < 3.0 {
					t.Errorf("step %d: mismatch shrank only %.3fx when the wavelength doubled; "+
						"O(a^2) needs ~4, so a Yang-Mills coefficient is wrong", i, r)
				}
			}
		} else {
			// control: the energy still contains the self-coupling while the
			// force no longer does, so the mismatch must NOT converge
			for _, r := range ratios {
				if r > 3.0 {
					t.Errorf("control converged at %.3fx -- the test is not actually "+
						"sensitive to the Yang-Mills terms", r)
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

The relative measure is unstable because at large amplitude the force passes through zero at individual sites. Switching to an RMS norm over many probes:

<details>
<summary>Tool Calls (2)</summary>

- **Bash**: `Ran `cd /Users/oreilly/wavereality/waves/wavesim && python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p="energy_test.go"; s=open(p).read()
i = s.index("// ewGradMismatch returns")
j = s.index("// TestElectroweakForceIsEnergyGradient")
s = s[:i] + r'''// ewProbes are the (site, adjoint, component) points the gradient check is
// evaluated at. A single probe is fragile: at large amplitude the force passes
// through zero at particular sites, and a RELATIVE error measured against a
// near-zero reference is meaningless. An RMS over many probes is stable.
func ewProbes(sz int32) [][5]int32 {
	var pr [][5]int32
	for _, c := range [][3]int32{{4, 4, 4}, {5, 4, 6}, {6, 5, 4}, {4, 6, 5}} {
		for a := int32(0); a < 3; a++ {
			for d := int32(0); d < 3; d++ {
				pr = append(pr, [5]int32{c[0], c[1], c[2], a, d})
			}
		}
	}
	return pr
}

// ewGradMismatch returns the RMS relative difference between the kernel's force
// and -dU/dphi over all probes, plus the RMS force scale.
func ewGradMismatch(sz int32, L float64, amp float32, ym bool) (float64, float64) {
	ss := ymSim(sz)
	ss.Params.YangMills.SetBool(ym)
	ss.Params.Update()
	ewFillWave(sz, L, amp)

	pr := ewProbes(sz)
	// one step gives every kernel force at once
	save := State.Clone()
	ewStep(ss)
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	fk := make([]float64, len(pr))
	for i, q := range pr {
		vv := int(EWW1Xv) + int(q[3])*8 + int(q[4])
		fk[i] = float64(State.Value(int(q[2]), int(q[1]), int(q[0]), vv, cur)) / float64(ss.Params.CSq)
	}
	State.CopyFrom(save)
	GetCtx(0).Init()

	const h = 1e-3
	var sd, sf float64
	for i, q := range pr {
		vs := int(EWW1Xs) + int(q[3])*8 + int(q[4])
		base := State.Value(int(q[2]), int(q[1]), int(q[0]), vs, 0)
		set := func(v float32) {
			for tt := range 2 {
				State.Set(v, int(q[2]), int(q[1]), int(q[0]), vs, tt)
			}
		}
		set(base + h)
		up := ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear(q[0], q[1], q[2])
		set(base - h)
		dn := ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear(q[0], q[1], q[2])
		set(base)
		fn := -(up - dn) / (2 * h)
		sd += (fk[i] - fn) * (fk[i] - fn)
		sf += fn * fn
	}
	n := float64(len(pr))
	return math.Sqrt(sd/n) / math.Sqrt(sf/n), math.Sqrt(sf / n)
}

package wavesim

import ("math"; "testing")

// kernel force RMS, and the RMS of the YM contribution alone
func ymFrac(sz int32, L float64, amp float32) (float64, float64) {
	get := func(ym bool) []float64 {
		ss := ymSim(sz); ss.Params.YangMills.SetBool(ym); ss.Params.Update()
		ewFillWave(sz, L, amp)
		pr := ewProbes(sz)
		ewStep(ss)
		cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
		o := make([]float64, len(pr))
		for i, q := range pr {
			vv := int(EWW1Xv) + int(q[3])*8 + int(q[4])
			o[i] = float64(State.Value(int(q[2]), int(q[1]), int(q[0]), vv, cur)) / float64(ss.Params.CSq)
		}
		return o
	}
	on, off := get(true), get(false)
	var st, sd float64
	for i := range on { st += on[i]*on[i]; sd += (on[i]-off[i])*(on[i]-off[i]) }
	n := float64(len(on))
	return math.Sqrt(st/n), math.Sqrt(sd/n)
}

func TestDbgAmp(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 10
	t.Logf("%6s %5s %13s %13s %11s %13s", "amp", "L", "RMS force", "RMS of YM", "YM frac", "mismatch")
	for _, amp := range []float32{0.02, 0.08} {
		for _, L := range []float64{8, 16, 32, 64} {
			f, ymr := ymFrac(sz, L, amp)
			rel, _ := ewGradMismatch(sz, L, amp, true)
			t.Logf("%6.3f %5.0f %13.4e %13.4e %11.4f %13.4e", amp, L, f, ymr, ymr/f, rel)
		}
	}
}
