p='maxwell.goal'
s=open(p).read()
o = """// StandingWave is two identical polarized packets sent at each other along X.
//
// Where they overlap E and B are both standing rather than travelling, and
// their nodes are a quarter wavelength apart: E vanishes where B is largest.
// That offset is the whole reason a standing wave stores energy without
// transporting it -- the Poynting vector E x B averages to zero.
func StandingWave(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	pos, vel, _, _ := emTransverse(ss)
	om := ss.LatticeFreq(ss.Config.Wavelength, 0)
	xl := float32(ss.Config.Size.X)
	ss.SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel, math32.X, xl*0.3, 1, 1, om, 0)
	ss.SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel, math32.X, xl*0.7, 1, -1, om, 0)
}"""
n = """// StandingWave fills the box with a sinusoidal vector potential and NO
// velocity, which is equal parts running each way: a standing wave.
//
// A = cos(kx) held still evolves as cos(kx) cos(wt), so E = -dA/dt goes as
// cos(kx) sin(wt) and B = curl A as sin(kx) cos(wt). Their nodes are a quarter
// wavelength apart -- E vanishes where B peaks -- and they are also a quarter
// PERIOD apart in time. That double offset is why a standing wave stores
// energy without transporting it: E x B averages to zero both ways.
//
// Edges wrap, so put a whole number of wavelengths in the box or the two ends
// will not meet.
func StandingWave(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	pos, _, _, _ := emTransverse(ss)
	ss.Sine(pos, math32.X, ss.Config.Wavelength, 0, ss.Config.Amplitude, 0)
	ss.CopyCurToPrev() // no velocity
}"""
assert o in s
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(o, n, 1))

p='maxwell_test.go'
s=open(p).read()

# --- polarized: two wavelengths, converging to c
a = s.index("// TestPolarizedPhoton")
b = s.index("// TestCircularPolarization")
n2 = '''// TestPolarizedPhoton: only the vector potential is set, and everything else
// follows. E must come out along the polarization, B along the other
// transverse direction, and nothing along the direction of travel.
//
// |E|/|B| is c only in the continuum: E comes from a time derivative whose
// lattice symbol is 2 sin(k/2) and B from a space derivative with a different
// one, so the ratio is c times a factor that goes to 1 as the wavelength grows.
// The test is that it converges, at the second-order rate.
func TestPolarizedPhoton(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 32
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name           string
		pol            math32.Dims
		wantE, wantB   EMStates
		otherE, otherB EMStates
	}{
		{"Y", math32.Y, EY, BZ, EZ, BY},
		{"Z", math32.Z, EZ, BY, EY, BZ},
	} {
		var errs [2]float64
		for wi, wl := range []float32{8, 16} {
			ss := emSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
				s.Config.Polarization = tc.pol
				s.Config.Wavelength = wl
				s.Config.PacketWidth = 2 * wl
				PolarizedPhoton(s)
			})
			for range 20 {
				emStep(ss)
			}
			e := emRMS(sz, tc.wantE)
			b := emRMS(sz, tc.wantB)
			eo := emRMS(sz, tc.otherE)
			bo := emRMS(sz, tc.otherB)
			ex := emRMS(sz, EX)
			bx := emRMS(sz, BX)
			c := float64(ss.Params.C)
			errs[wi] = math.Abs(e/b/c - 1)
			t.Logf("%s-polarized wl=%2.0f: |%v|=%.4f |%v|=%.4f  E/B=%.4f (c=%.2f, %+.1f%%)   other transverse %.1e/%.1e  along travel %.1e/%.1e",
				tc.name, wl, tc.wantE, e, tc.wantB, b, e/b, c, 100*(e/b/c-1), eo, bo, ex, bx)
			if eo > 1e-6*e || bo > 1e-6*b {
				t.Errorf("%s: the other transverse direction is not empty: E %g B %g", tc.name, eo, bo)
			}
			if ex > 1e-6*e || bx > 1e-6*b {
				t.Errorf("%s: something along the direction of travel: E %g B %g", tc.name, ex, bx)
			}
		}
		if errs[1] > 0.4*errs[0] {
			t.Errorf("%s: |E|/|B| error %.3f -> %.3f on doubling the wavelength, want 4x better",
				tc.name, errs[0], errs[1])
		}
	}
}

'''

n4 = '''// TestStandingWave: in a travelling wave E and B rise and fall together; in a
// standing one their nodes are a quarter wavelength apart, so where one is
// large the other is small.
func TestStandingWave(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 48
	corr := func(init func(*Sim), nst int) float64 {
		ss := emSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Config.Wavelength = 8 // 6 whole wavelengths in the box
			s.Config.PacketWidth = 40
			init(s)
		})
		for range nst {
			emStep(ss)
		}
		e := emLine(sz, EY, sz/2, sz/2)
		b := emLine(sz, BZ, sz/2, sz/2)
		var se, sb, see, sbb, seb, n float64
		for x := range int(sz) {
			ea, ba := math.Abs(e[x]), math.Abs(b[x])
			se += ea
			sb += ba
			see += ea * ea
			sbb += ba * ba
			seb += ea * ba
			n++
		}
		cov := seb/n - (se/n)*(sb/n)
		return cov / math.Sqrt((see/n-(se/n)*(se/n))*(sbb/n-(sb/n)*(sb/n)))
	}
	trav := corr(PolarizedPhoton, 5)
	stand := corr(StandingWave, 5)
	t.Logf("correlation of |E| with |B| along X: travelling %+.3f, standing %+.3f", trav, stand)
	if trav < 0.9 {
		t.Errorf("travelling wave: |E| and |B| should move together, got %g", trav)
	}
	if stand > -0.5 {
		t.Errorf("standing wave: |E| and |B| nodes should be a quarter wave apart, got %g", stand)
	}
}

'''
s = s.replace(o, n4, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)

Six Maxwell configs, a radial stat, and 5 new tests — 35 passing, 14 validations, everything builds.

## The configs

**Electric Potential** — a point charge at `Config.Source`, relaxing to the Coulomb field. `A0NoWave` makes the A0 update Jacobi relaxation of Poisson rather than a wave, so it fills in and settles.

```
X r= 2.0: A0 0.65832  fit -0.4%     |E| r=4->6: power 1.92 (want 2)
X r= 4.0: A0 0.28504  fit +2.4%     D |E| r=4->6: power 2.03
X r= 6.0: A0 0.15141  fit +0.4%
anisotropy at r=4: axis 0.28504 diag 0.28739  ratio 0.9918
anisotropy at r=6: axis 0.15141 diag 0.15260  ratio 0.9921
```

**0.8% axis-vs-diagonal** on a field that should be perfectly spherical — that's your 19-point stencil earning its keep, measured directly.

Edges are **fixed**, not damped: that grounds the walls, so the solution is the Dirichlet form $k(1/r - 1/R)$ rather than 1/r plus an arbitrary floating constant. Damped walls gave A0 flattening out around 0.42 instead of falling.

**Polarized Photon / Circular Polarization** — you had it right. Only $\vec A$ is set, in one transverse component, and everything else follows from the kernel:

```
Y-polarized: |EY|=0.2150 |BZ|=0.3573   other transverse 0.0e+00/0.0e+00   along travel 0.0e+00/1.4e-09
Z-polarized: |EZ|=0.2150 |BY|=0.3573
```

E along the polarization, B along the *other* transverse direction, exactly zero in the third — both the unused transverse component and the direction of travel. Two transverse choices, and that's all polarization is for a plane wave. A longitudinal one isn't available to pick, and that's not an omission: setting AX is pure gauge, E = B = 0.

Circular is just those two a quarter cycle apart. The measurement that makes it click:

```
|E_transverse|^2 ripple over one wavelength: linear 1.000, circular 0.010
```

A linear wave's E swings to zero twice a wavelength; the circular one's has constant magnitude and only turns. It isn't a third kind of wave — it's two linear ones with a phase offset, which is why any polarization can be written in either basis.

**Standing Wave** — I changed this from two colliding packets to a sinusoid held with zero velocity, which is cleaner and exactly equal parts running each way. `|E|`/`|B|` correlation: **+0.980 travelling, −0.886 standing**. Nodes a quarter wavelength apart, so E×B averages to zero and nothing is transported.

**Moving Charge** — the honest answer to your question. This kernel has no advection, so a localized charge can't actually move. The one configuration where that doesn't matter is a uniformly charged line sliding along *itself*: the density it leaves behind is the density it had, so continuity holds exactly and it's a genuine current.

```
at rest:  E_y = +0.89500, B_z = +0.00000e+00
v=0.25 r=2: E_y=+1.03706 B_z=+1.04932  B/E=1.0118 (want v/c^2 = 1.0000)
v=0.25 r=3: B/E=1.0150
v=0.25 r=8: B/E=1.2168
```

At rest B is **exactly zero**; moving, it circulates (sign of $\hat x \times \hat y$) with |B|/|E| = v/c² to 1%. Magnetism is what electric charge looks like when it moves, with the conversion factor right there.

**Charge Dipole** — two opposite charges; far field falls as 1/r³ because the potentials cancel to leading order.

## Infrastructure

`StatRadial` / `StatRadialVec` sample any variable at multiples of `Config.Wavelength` from `Config.Source`, along +X and the (1,1,1) diagonal. `MaxwellStats` wires up A0, |E|, |B| plus group velocity for AY/AZ, and `waves.go` now calls it. `Config` gained `Source` and `Polarization`; `SlabPacket` is now `enums.Enum` with a `phase` argument (that's what makes circular polarization one extra call), and `ewFreq` is promoted to `Sim.LatticeFreq`.

Also fixed `MaxwellShouldDisplay`, which listed `"A0Velocity"` — a field that no longer exists, so that toggle wasn't showing.

## Three things worth flagging

**I had a measurement bug that looked like physics.** The first isotropy run showed the diagonal 26–30% above the axis. That was `CoordToInt` truncating, which shortens a diagonal radius by up to 13%. `StateAtInterp` (trilinear) fixed it and the anisotropy dropped to 0.8%. Worth knowing because the same trap is waiting in any radial measurement.

**|E|/|B| is not exactly c on the lattice** — it's +20% at wavelength 8, +8% at 16. E comes from a time derivative whose symbol is $2\sin(k/2)$ and B from a space derivative with a different one. The test asserts second-order convergence rather than equality, which is the honest claim.

**The 1/r fit and isotropy check stop at r=6 of a 12-cube half-width.** Past that the grounded wall distorts things — and a *cubical* wall is 12 cubes away along the axis but 21 along the diagonal, so no single R describes both. Beyond that radius the test logs the numbers but doesn't assert on them.

Mostly yes — parts 2 and 3 are right, and part 3 is right for a deeper reason than you gave. But part 1 has the gauge label backwards, and interestingly your own sentence about Coulomb gauge later in the question is the correct one.

## A0NoWave is the Coulomb condition, not Lorenz

I tested it directly — a bump in A0 with no charge anywhere:

```
wave  (A0NoWave=false) step 10: A0 center -0.26977, A0 at r=12 +0.006276
wave                   step 20: A0 center +0.00006, A0 at r=12 +0.040099
wave                   step 30: A0 center +0.00000, A0 at r=12 -0.033593

relax (A0NoWave=true)  step 10: A0 center +0.27445, A0 at r=12 +0.000470
relax                  step 20: A0 center +0.15387, A0 at r=12 +0.002481
relax                  step 30: A0 center +0.10151, A0 at r=12 +0.004765
```

With the flag off, the bump **leaves** — gone from the center by step 20, and what arrives at r=12 rings (+0.040, −0.034). That's $\Box A_0 = \rho/\varepsilon_0$, the Lorenz-gauge wave equation, propagating at c.

With it on, the bump **decays in place** and spreads monotonically. Setting velocity = force makes the update $A_0 \mathrel{+}= c^2\nabla^2 A_0 + \rho/\varepsilon_0$, which is Jacobi iteration converging to $\nabla^2 A_0 = -\rho/\varepsilon_0$ — Poisson. No time derivative, no propagation. That is the **Coulomb** gauge condition for the scalar potential. Your `ElectricPotential` test result, $A_0 = k(1/r - 1/R)$, is that Poisson solution.

So the `// Lorentz gauge` comment in `MaxwellKernel` mislabels it — and also spells it for Hendrik Lorentz rather than Ludvig Lorenz, who are different people. The `C < 1` half of the comment is right: Jacobi with the normalized 19-point stencil needs $c^2 < 1$.

**The caveat worth knowing.** The A sector still assumes Lorenz — $\Box \vec A = \mu_0\vec J$ reproduces Ampère–Maxwell only if $\nabla\cdot\vec A + \dot A_0/c^2 = 0$. Meanwhile `A0NoWave` imposes the Coulomb condition on $A_0$. Both hold together only when $\dot A_0 = 0$ and $\nabla\cdot\vec A$ is constant — static or quasi-static, or a transverse current. Every Maxwell config I added sits in that regime (that's partly why `MovingCharge` is a line current: $\nabla\cdot\vec J = 0$ exactly). Where it bites is the electroweak kernel, where the Higgs current is dynamical and generally not divergence-free — so `A0NoWave` there buys stability at the cost of exact gauge consistency. Given that the alternative was the secular runaway, that's the right trade, but it's a trade.

## The 2 DOF are direction-dependent — yes, exactly right

4 components − 1 gauge condition − 1 residual gauge freedom = 2. But *which* two are physical is set by $\hat k$. For a wave along x the physical pair is $(A_y, A_z)$ and $(A_0, A_x)$ is the gauge pair; rotate the wave to travel along y and $A_x$ becomes physical while $A_y$ becomes longitudinal.

Your own test data says this: `PolarizedPhoton` gives E and B **exactly zero** along the direction of travel, and setting $A_x$ instead of a transverse component would give $E = B = 0$ — pure gauge, nothing there. Yet in `StandingWave`, with waves going both ways, every component is doing something.

There's a sharper version of your point that matters for the cellular-automaton goal: transversality is $\vec k \cdot \vec A = 0$, and projecting onto it in position space is **non-local** — it needs $1/\nabla^2$. So a strictly local update rule *cannot* carry only the two physical DOF. The redundancy is the price of locality, not sloppiness in the formulation.

## A0 is constrained, not dynamical — right, and here's the real reason

You framed it as "clamped by external sources." True, but the structural reason is stronger: **$A_0$ has no conjugate momentum**. The Lagrangian $-\tfrac14 F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ contains no $\partial_t A_0$ anywhere — $F_{00} = 0$, and $F_{0i} = \partial_t A_i - \partial_i A_0$ has only $\partial_t A_i$. So $\pi^0 \equiv 0$ identically. That's a primary constraint. $A_0$'s equation of motion is Gauss's law, which is a constraint on initial data, not an evolution equation. It needs no initial value and has no independent time development in *any* gauge.

One refinement: in Lorenz gauge $A_0$ *looks* dynamical — it obeys a wave equation, as the run above shows. That's an artifact of the gauge-fixing term, which adds $-\tfrac{1}{2\xi}(\partial\cdot A)^2$ and gives $\pi^0 = -(\partial\cdot A)/\xi \neq 0$. Those propagating $A_0$ modes carry no energy: they cancel exactly against the longitudinal $A$ modes, which is Gupta–Bleuler in the quantum theory. So "$A_0$ is not a real DOF" survives Lorenz gauge — the apparent dynamics is spurious.

Which ties the whole thing together: that spurious scalar–longitudinal sector is precisely what ran away on you in the electroweak kernel. `A0NoWave` works because it deletes the artifact rather than trying to keep it cancelled numerically.

Want me to fix the gauge comment in `MaxwellKernel` and add the consistency caveat to the `A0NoWave` parameter doc? One-line change plus a short note.

  In [[Klein-Gordon]] we saw that a major problem with the scalar KG equation is that it doesn't represent any kind of conserved value: you cannot compute some constant, unchanging value from the $\phi$ state variables under this equation. This is a problem if you want to develop a probabilistic interpretation of the wave, as in [[Schrodinger]]'s equation for the standard [[Copenhagen]] interpretation. But it is also a problem for other interpretations as well. See [[conservation]] for an essential overview.
  
  In particular, we would like the KG waves to represent **waves of charge** (i.e., [[matter wave]]s), because charge is also strictly conserved, and it comes in both positive and negative varieties, which the KG waves produce. By contrast, the Schrödinger wave only represents a positive-valued quantity, which fits better with the probabilistic interpretation. Indeed, the authors that do write extensively about the KG equation adopt this interpretation ([[@Greiner00]]; [[@Gingrich04]]; [[@MandlShaw13]]), and this idea was pursued initially by Schrödinger in 1926. Furthermore, we will see that this charge interpretation fits naturally with the coupling of this KG equation to the electromagnetic (EM) field ([[Maxwell]]'s equations), where the conserved charge value acts just like the electric charge in driving the field. 
  
  The critical step for transforming the KG equation into something that can represent a conserved charge value is to simply have it operate on wave state with [[complex number]]s instead of scalars! The reason is at once simple and yet deeply profound for the nature of the quantum realm:
  
  > Complex numbers naturally maintain a constant radius as they rotate around the complex plane.

  Interestingly, this is actually a good model of how the [[Higgs]] mechanism works, because it involves precisely such a coupling between a spinless complex field and the gauge vector boson field $B^\mu$ that works just like the electromagnetic four-potential $A^\mu$.
  
  However, to model the behavior of [[fermion]] particles, the wave function needs [[spin]], which is what the [[Dirac]] wave function adds on top of the KG waves. This coupling of charge waves and EM waves has been pursued more recently in neoclassical self-coupled field theory ([[@JaynesCummings63]]; [[@CrispJaynes69]]; [[@BarutVanHuele85]]; [[@BarutDowling90]]; [[@Crisp96]]; [[@FinsterSmollerYau99a]]; [[@Radford03]]; [[@MasielloDeumensOhrn05]]). It is pedagogically useful to incrementally develop this scalar (non-spinning) version of electrodynamic interactions first, and then introduce the further complexities of spin in the [[Dirac]] equation.
  
  ## Complex state and conserved charge
  
  The first step is to introduce a wave state with [[complex number]]s ($\chi$) instead of scalars ($\phi$), which then supports the computation of a conserved quantity across the two complex state values. When we translate this complex wave function into two separate second-order wave equations without an $i$ imaginary number factor, the KG equation is identical to computing two separate KG equations on each of the two scalar values represented by the complex state variable (i.e., $\phi_a$ and $\phi_b$). This is different from Schrödinger's wave equation, which is first order and has an $i$ term that causes the $a$ and $b$ terms to intermix as the wave unfolds.
  
  {id="eq_kg-complex" title="Klein-Gordon on complex state"}
  $$
  \frac{\partial^2 \chi}{\partial t^2} = (\nabla^2 - m_0^2) \chi
  $$
  
  Because differentiation operates independently on the two separate scalar variables in a complex number, this is equivalent to two parallel scalar KG equations, which we can write as:
  
  $$
  \frac{\partial^2 \phi_a}{\partial t^2} = \left( \nabla^2 - m_0^2 \right) \phi_a
  $$

  [[#sim_cc]] demonstrates how this works, in terms of two simple [[harmonic oscillator]] variables _a_ and _b_, which are set to be a specific phase apart from each other (+90 degrees shifts _b_ to the _left_ (earlier) relative to _a_, while -90 shifts to the right, due to the trigonometric convention of 0 degrees being at 1,0 and proceeding counter-clockwise from there). Regardless of the phase relationship, the computed charge value remains constant across the cycles of oscillation. However, critically, the value of the charge is directly a function of this phase relationship, with a maximum of 0.5 when the _b_ value is +90 degrees in relation to the _a_ value, and a minimum of -0.5 for -90 degrees, and zero for 0 or 180 degrees. These relationships are fairly obvious once you appreciate the relationship between velocity and position for each of the variables (which are 90 degrees out of phase with each other, always), and how they enter into the charge equation.
  
  Critically, complex numbers are _always_ 90 degrees out of phase with each other by the very nature of the complex plane. Thus, even though the separate real-valued wave functions are independently updated, it is critical that these two wave states are _initialized_ with the 90 degree phase relationship appropriate for complex numbers, which will then determine the sign of the charge value represented.
  
  Perhaps the most important feature of this charge equation is that it can be either positive or negative, as a function of the phase relationship. This is not true of the corresponding expression for Schrödinger's equation, which is "definitely positive", or, in mathematical terminology, "positive definite". This is one of the major reasons why standard quantum physics has strongly embraced Schrödinger's equation, and not KG: KG does not fit with the standard probabilistic framework, where the wave describes a probability, and a probability is always positive.
  
  Interestingly, the Dirac equation, which is used in the [[Standard Model]] for all [[fermion]] particles such as the [[electron]], also produces negative "probabilities", but these have been (correctly, in our framework) reinterpreted as representing antiparticles (i.e., particles with an opposite charge). The antiparticle of the electron is the **positron**, and it is just like an electron, except it has the opposite charge. Historically, this antiparticle nature of the Dirac equation was regarded as a major problem, until positrons were subsequently discovered, and then Dirac looked like a genius for having made such a bold prediction.
  
  We can also derive an expression for the motion of charge over space, which is the _charge current density_ $\vec{J}$:
  
  {id="eq_kg-current" title="Klein-Gordon current density"}
  $$
  \vec{J} \equiv - \frac{i \hbar e}{2m_0} \left( \chi^* \vec{\nabla} \chi - \chi \vec{\nabla} \chi^* \right)
  $$
  
  In terms of the underlying scalar state variables (and again for natural units), this is:
  
  $$
  \vec{J} = \frac{e}{m_0} (\phi_a \vec{\nabla} \phi_b - \phi_b \vec{\nabla} \phi_a)
  $$

  In the electromagnetic field equations, the driving force from charge $\rho$ adds into the second-order temporal derivative $\frac{\partial^2 {}}{\partial t^2}$ ([[maxwell#eq_scalar-pot-chg]] in [[Maxwell]]):
  
  $$
  \frac{\partial^2 {A_0}}{\partial t^2} = \nabla^2 A_0 + \frac{1}{\epsilon_0} \rho
  $$
  
  However, in Schrödinger's equation, external forces enter as a potential ($V$), in the first-order derivative  $\frac{\partial {}}{\partial t}$:
  
  $$
  i \hbar \frac{\partial {\chi}}{\partial t} = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \chi + V \chi
  $$
  
  This makes sense, because force is the derivative of a potential, so potential is a first-order factor, and force is a second-order factor.
  
  Our KG (Klein-Gordon) charge wave equation is a second-order equation, expressed in terms of $\frac{\partial^2 {}}{\partial t^2}$, and therefore we need to include external driving forces, not potentials. However, for various reasons, it is necessary to derive such an equation starting from the potential. To do this, we can re-derive a second-order wave equation by replacing the first-order derivative with the following first-order _covariant_ derivative operator $D$, that subtracts the external driving potential:
  
  $$
  D_\mu \def \partial_\mu - i \frac{e}{c} A^\mu
  $$

n = '''// KleinGordonCKernel is the kernel for the complex Klein-Gordon equation, with
// optional minimal coupling to the electromagnetic field (Params.EM).
//
// Uncoupled, the two components evolve as two independent real KG waves: the
// complex structure only shows up in the conserved charge, which needs both.
//
// Coupled, the covariant derivative D = d - i(e/hbar)A adds three terms:
//
//	dd(phi_a) = c^2 (Lap - mhsq) phi_a + (2e/hbar)(A0 d(phi_b) + c A.grad phi_b) + (e^2/hbar^2)(A0^2 - A^2) phi_a
//	dd(phi_b) = c^2 (Lap - mhsq) phi_b - (2e/hbar)(A0 d(phi_a) + c A.grad phi_a) + (e^2/hbar^2)(A0^2 - A^2) phi_b
//
// The A0 term acts on the VELOCITY with opposite signs on the two components,
// which is a rotation of (d phi_a, d phi_b) at rate 2 e A0 / hbar. An explicit
// integrator does not rotate, it spirals, and the charge runs away -- which is
// the instability described in web/content/complex-kg.md. Params.Boris applies
// the rotation exactly instead. See EWBorisPhase for the same problem in the
// electroweak kernel.
//
// It also writes the [Charge] and [Current] that MaxwellKernel reads, so the
// wave and the field drive each other.
func KleinGordonCKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	ok := ctx.StateCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if !ok {
		return
	}
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	pposA := State[z, y, x, CabPosA, prv]
	pposB := State[z, y, x, CabPosB, prv]
	pvelA := State[z, y, x, CabVelA, prv]
	pvelB := State[z, y, x, CabVelB, prv]
	vpot := State[z, y, x, CabV, prv]

	mhsq := Params[0].MOverHSq
	csq := Params[0].CSq
	threeD := Params[0].ThreeD.IsTrue()

	var forceA, forceB float32
	if threeD {
		forceA = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(CabPosA), prv, pposA)
		forceB = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(CabPosB), prv, pposB)
	} else {
		forceA = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(CabPosA), prv, pposA)
		forceB = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(CabPosB), prv, pposB)
	}
	forceA += (vpot - mhsq) * pposA // this is the only diff from standard Wave
	forceB += (vpot - mhsq) * pposB
	accA := csq * forceA
	accB := csq * forceB

	em := Params[0].EM.IsTrue()
	var a0, ax, ay, az, omega float32
	var gA, gB math32.Vector3
	if em {
		a0 = State[z, y, x, A0s, prv]
		ax = State[z, y, x, AXs, prv]
		ay = State[z, y, x, AYs, prv]
		az = State[z, y, x, AZs, prv]
		if threeD {
			gA = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(CabPosA), prv)
			gB = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(CabPosB), prv)
		} else {
			gA = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(CabPosA), prv)
			gB = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(CabPosB), prv)
		}
		e2h := Params[0].E2OverH
		cc := Params[0].C
		asq := a0*a0 - (ax*ax + ay*ay + az*az)
		eh2 := Params[0].EOverHSq * asq
		accA += e2h*cc*(ax*gB.X+ay*gB.Y+az*gB.Z) + eh2*pposA
		accB += -e2h*cc*(ax*gA.X+ay*gA.Y+az*gA.Z) + eh2*pposB
		omega = e2h * a0 // the A0 rotation rate
	}

	var velA, velB float32
	if em && Params[0].Boris.IsTrue() {
		// half kick, exact rotation, half kick. d(v_a + i v_b)/dt =
		// -i omega (v_a + i v_b), so the velocity turns by -omega per step.
		haA := 0.5 * accA
		haB := 0.5 * accB
		mA := pvelA + haA
		mB := pvelB + haB
		cs := math32.Cos(omega)
		sn := math32.Sin(omega)
		velA = cs*mA + sn*mB + haA
		velB = -sn*mA + cs*mB + haB
	} else {
		velA = pvelA + accA + omega*pvelB
		velB = pvelB + accB - omega*pvelA
	}
	posA := pposA + velA
	posB := pposB + velB

	// charge and current, at the same time as the position they use: the
	// midpoint velocity is the one that belongs with the previous position in
	// a leapfrog, and the gradients are of the previous position too.
	midA := 0.5 * (pvelA + velA)
	midB := 0.5 * (pvelB + velB)
	ccm := pposA*pposA + pposB*pposB
	hem := 2 * Params[0].HEOver2MCSq // hbar e / (m c^2)
	rho := hem * (pposB*midA - pposA*midB)
	if em {
		rho -= Params[0].EsqOverMCSq * a0 * ccm
	} else if threeD {
		gA = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(CabPosA), prv)
		gB = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(CabPosB), prv)
	} else {
		gA = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(CabPosA), prv)
		gB = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(CabPosB), prv)
	}
	jf := hem * csq // hbar e / m
	jx := jf * (pposA*gB.X - pposB*gA.X)
	jy := jf * (pposA*gB.Y - pposB*gA.Y)
	jz := jf * (pposA*gB.Z - pposB*gA.Z)
	if em {
		ja := Params[0].EsqOverMCSq * Params[0].C * ccm
		jx -= ja * ax
		jy -= ja * ay
		jz -= ja * az
	}
	State[z, y, x, Charge, cur] = rho
	State[z, y, x, CurrentX, cur] = jx
	State[z, y, x, CurrentY, cur] = jy
	State[z, y, x, CurrentZ, cur] = jz

	if Params[0].Energy.IsTrue() {
		midVel := 0.25 * (pvelA + velA + pvelB + velB)
		kinetic := Params[0].Inv2CSq * midVel * midVel
		var potential float32
		if threeD {
			potential = PotentialEnergy19(x, y, z, int32(CabPosA), prv, pposA) + PotentialEnergy19(x, y, z, int32(CabPosB), prv, pposB)
		} else {
			potential = PotentialEnergy1D(x, y, z, int32(CabPosA), prv, pposA) + PotentialEnergy1D(x, y, z, int32(CabPosB), prv, pposB)
		}
		State[z, y, x, CabKinetic, cur] = kinetic
		State[z, y, x, CabPotential, cur] = potential
		State[z, y, x, CabEnergy, cur] = kinetic + potential
	}
	State[z, y, x, CabCC, cur] = posA*posA + posB*posB
	State[z, y, x, CabForceA, cur] = forceA
	State[z, y, x, CabVelA, cur] = velA
	State[z, y, x, CabPosA, cur] = posA

	State[z, y, x, CabForceB, cur] = forceB
	State[z, y, x, CabVelB, cur] = velB
	State[z, y, x, CabPosB, cur] = posB
}

'''
s = s[:a] + n + s[b:]
s = s.replace('''package wavesim

//gosl:start''', '''package wavesim

import "cogentcore.org/core/math32"

//gosl:start''', 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")

//////// configurations

// ChargeAtRest fills space with a uniform complex wave turning at the rest
// mass frequency: a charge density with no motion.
//
// Uniform means the Laplacian vanishes, so each component is a plain harmonic
// oscillator at Omega0 = m c^2 / hbar, and the two of them a quarter cycle
// apart are a complex number rotating at that rate. The charge
//
//	rho = (hbar e / m c^2) (phi_b d phi_a - phi_a d phi_b)
//
// is then exactly -e |chi|^2 and does not change, which is the whole point of
// going complex: no single real field has a conserved quantity like this.
//
// Reverse the sense of rotation and the charge changes sign, with nothing else
// about the wave any different. That is antimatter, in the only sense this
// equation knows about it.
func ChargeAtRest(ss *Sim) {
	ss.ChargedUniform(ss.Config.Amplitude, 1)
}

// ChargeAtRestAnti is [ChargeAtRest] turning the other way: the same wave with
// the opposite charge.
func ChargeAtRestAnti(ss *Sim) {
	ss.ChargedUniform(ss.Config.Amplitude, -1)
}

// ChargedPacket is a moving charge: a wave packet in the two components a
// quarter wavelength apart, travelling along X.
func ChargedPacket(ss *Sim) {
	ss.ChargedPacketConfig(math32.X, ss.Config.Amplitude, 1)
}

	InitFunc{Name: "Charged Packet", Doc: "A moving charge: a complex wave packet travelling along X, carrying charge and current", Func: ChargedPacket},
}

// KGCConfigs stats plotted over time in the GUI.

	ss.AddStat(ss.StatSum(CabCC))

	ss.Fill(CabPosA, Both, amp)
	ss.Fill(CabVelB, Both, sign*ss.Params.Omega0*amp)

	ss.MovingWavePacketConfig(CabPosA, CabVelA, dim, ctr, 1, 0, amp)
	ss.MovingWavePacketConfig(CabPosB, CabVelB, dim, ctr, 1, sign*0.25, amp)
}

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"
)

// kgSim builds a 3D complex Klein-Gordon sim.
func kgSim(sz int32, init func(*Sim)) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU = false
	ss.Config.GUI = false
	ss.Config.Equation = KleinGordonC
	ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, sz, sz)
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.ThreeD.SetBool(true)
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.StateVars = CabStatesN
	ss.ConfigState()
	ss.KleinGordonCStats()
	ss.InitFunc = init
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

func kgStep(ss *Sim) {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	ctx.StepInc()
	ns := int(ctx.Size.X * ctx.Size.Y * ctx.Size.Z)
	if ss.Params.EM.IsTrue() {
		RunMaxwellKernel(ns)
	}
	RunKleinGordonCKernel(ns)
	if ss.Params.Edges == EdgesWrap {
		RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
	}
	ss.RunStats(false)
}

func kgSum(sz int32, vr CabStates) float64 {
	return StateSum(GetCtx(0).Size.V(), vr, GetCtx(0).CurState)
}

// TestKGChargeConserved: with no field, the total charge must not change at
// all. This is the property the complex version exists to have -- the real
// scalar KG equation has nothing like it.
func TestKGChargeConserved(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 8
	ss := kgSim(sz, ChargedPacket)
	kgStep(ss)
	q0 := kgSum(sz, Charge)
	var lo, hi float64 = q0, q0
	for range 2000 {
		kgStep(ss)
		q := kgSum(sz, Charge)
		lo, hi = math.Min(lo, q), math.Max(hi, q)
	}
	t.Logf("free packet: total charge %.6e, drift over 2000 steps %.2e (relative %.2e)",
		q0, hi-lo, (hi-lo)/math.Abs(q0))
	if math.Abs(q0) < 1e-9 {
		t.Fatalf("packet carries no charge at all: %g", q0)
	}
	if (hi-lo)/math.Abs(q0) > 1e-5 {
		t.Errorf("charge not conserved: range %g on %g", hi-lo, q0)
	}
}

// TestKGChargeSign: the sign of the charge is the direction the complex phase
// turns, and nothing else. Same |chi|^2, opposite charge -- which is the only
// difference between a particle and its antiparticle here.
func TestKGChargeSign(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 6
	var q [2]float64
	var cc [2]float64
	for i, init := range []func(*Sim){ChargeAtRest, ChargeAtRestAnti} {
		ss := kgSim(sz, init)
		kgStep(ss)
		q[i] = kgSum(sz, Charge)
		cc[i] = kgSum(sz, CabCC)
		// the analytic value: rho = -sign e amp^2 per cell
		amp := float64(ss.Config.Amplitude)
		n := float64(sz * sz * sz)
		want := -float64(ss.Params.E) * amp * amp * n
		if i == 1 {
			want = -want
		}
		t.Logf("%-20s total charge %+.5f (want %+.5f), |chi|^2 %.5f",
			[]string{"ChargeAtRest", "ChargeAtRestAnti"}[i], q[i], want, cc[i])
		if math.Abs(q[i]/want-1) > 0.02 {
			t.Errorf("charge %g, want %g", q[i], want)
		}
	}
	if q[0]*q[1] >= 0 {
		t.Errorf("the two rotation senses should have opposite charge: %g and %g", q[0], q[1])
	}
	if math.Abs(cc[0]/cc[1]-1) > 1e-6 {
		t.Errorf("they should be the same wave: |chi|^2 %g vs %g", cc[0], cc[1])
	}
}

// TestKGContinuity: charge is conserved locally, not just globally --
// d(rho)/dt + div J = 0. Checked as a convergence statement, since the
// discrete derivatives only agree to order h^2.
func TestKGContinuity(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 16
	var res [2]float64
	for i, wl := range []float32{4, 8} {
		ss := kgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Config.Wavelength = wl
			s.Config.PacketWidth = 2 * wl
			ChargedPacket(s)
		})
		ctx := GetCtx(0)
		kgStep(ss)
		prev := make([]float64, 0, sz*sz*sz)
		cur := int(ctx.CurState)
		for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
			for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
				for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
					prev = append(prev, float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(Charge), cur)))
				}
			}
		}
		kgStep(ss)
		cur = int(ctx.CurState)
		var resid, scale float64
		k := 0
		for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
			for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
				for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
					rho := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(Charge), cur))
					drho := rho - prev[k]
					var dx, dy, dz float32
					div := Divergence10(x, y, z, int32(CurrentX), int32(cur), &dx, &dy, &dz)
					resid += (drho + float64(div)) * (drho + float64(div))
					scale += float64(div) * float64(div)
					k++
				}
			}
		}
		res[i] = math.Sqrt(resid / scale)
		t.Logf("wavelength %2.0f: RMS of (d rho/dt + div J) is %.3f of RMS div J", wl, res[i])
	}
	if res[1] > 0.4*res[0] {
		t.Errorf("continuity residual %.3f -> %.3f on doubling the wavelength, want 4x better",
			res[0], res[1])
	}
}

p='init.goal'
s=open(p).read()
o = """// ChargedPacketConfig adds a travelling complex wave packet along dim, with
// the two components a quarter wavelength apart so it carries charge. Takes
// its wavelength and width from [Config]. sign picks the sign of the charge.
func (ss *Sim) ChargedPacketConfig(dim math32.Dims, amp, sign float32) {
	ctr := math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1)
	ss.MovingWavePacketConfig(CabPosA, CabVelA, dim, ctr, 1, 0, amp)
	ss.MovingWavePacketConfig(CabPosB, CabVelB, dim, ctr, 1, sign*0.25, amp)
}"""
n = """// ChargedPacketConfig adds a travelling complex wave packet along dim, with
// the two components a quarter cycle apart so it carries charge. Takes its
// wavelength and width from [Config]. sign picks the sign of the charge.
//
// Built from [Sim.SlabPacket] at the exact lattice frequency for this mass, so
// it is a clean positive-frequency packet running one way: chi = env e^i(kx -
// wt), for which rho is env^2 times a constant. [Sim.MovingWavePacket] would
// be the obvious choice but its velocity comes from fitted constants tuned for
// massless waves, so the packet it makes is not a KG eigenstate and splits.
func (ss *Sim) ChargedPacketConfig(dim math32.Dims, amp, sign float32) {
	wl := ss.Config.Wavelength
	om := ss.LatticeFreq(wl, math32.Sqrt(ss.Params.MOverHSq))
	ctr := float32(ss.Config.Size.Dim(dim)) * 0.5
	wd := ss.Config.PacketWidth
	ss.SlabPacket(CabPosA, CabVelA, dim, ctr, wl, wd, amp, 1, om, 0)
	ss.SlabPacket(CabPosB, CabVelB, dim, ctr, wl, wd, amp, 1, om, -sign*0.5*math32.Pi)
}"""
assert o in s

// kgStepExt advances the wave in a FIXED external field: no Maxwell kernel, so
// A0 and A stay exactly as initialized.
func kgStepExt(ss *Sim) {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	ctx.StepInc()
	RunKleinGordonCKernel(int(ctx.Size.X * ctx.Size.Y * ctx.Size.Z))
	if ss.Params.Edges == EdgesWrap {
		RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
	}
	ss.RunStats(false)
}

// TestKGGaugeUniform: a uniform constant A0 is pure gauge -- it multiplies chi
// by a phase and changes no observable. Both |chi|^2 and the total charge must
// come out the same as with no field at all.
//
// The charge is the sharper half. The free part alone is NOT invariant: the
// phase rotation adds to phi_b d(phi_a) - phi_a d(phi_b). The -e^2 A0 |chi|^2
// term in rho is exactly what cancels that, so this tests that the coupling
// term in the CHARGE matches the coupling term in the EQUATION.
func TestKGGaugeUniform(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 6
	run := func(a0 float32) (q, cc float64) {
		ss := kgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			if a0 != 0 {
				s.Params.EM.SetBool(true)
				s.Params.Update()
			}
			ChargeAtRest(s)
			s.Fill(A0s, Both, a0)
		})
		for range 200 {
			kgStepExt(ss)
		}
		return kgSum(sz, Charge), kgSum(sz, CabCC)
	}
	q0, cc0 := run(0)
	for _, a0 := range []float32{0.05, 0.2} {
		q, cc := run(a0)
		t.Logf("A0 = %.2f: total charge %+.5f (free %+.5f, %+.2e)   |chi|^2 %.5f (free %.5f, %+.2e)",
			a0, q, q0, q/q0-1, cc, cc0, cc/cc0-1)
		if math.Abs(q/q0-1) > 1e-3 {
			t.Errorf("A0 = %g changed the charge by %.2e: a uniform A0 is pure gauge", a0, q/q0-1)
		}
		if math.Abs(cc/cc0-1) > 1e-3 {
			t.Errorf("A0 = %g changed |chi|^2 by %.2e", a0, cc/cc0-1)
		}
	}
}

// TestKGBorisStability: the A0 coupling turns the velocity (d phi_a, d phi_b)
// at rate 2 e A0 / hbar. An explicit step does not turn it, it spirals out,
// and the wave grows without bound -- the instability that
// web/content/complex-kg.md describes and works around by updating the two
// components in sequence. Params.Boris applies the rotation exactly instead.
func TestKGBorisStability(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 6
	run := func(boris bool) []float64 {
		ss := kgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Params.EM.SetBool(true)
			s.Params.Boris.SetBool(boris)
			s.Params.Update()
			ChargeAtRest(s)
			s.Fill(A0s, Both, 0.5) // a big field, to make the point quickly
		})
		var out []float64
		for i := range 2000 {
			kgStepExt(ss)
			if (i+1)%500 == 0 {
				out = append(out, kgSum(sz, CabCC))
			}
		}
		return out
	}
	off := run(false)
	on := run(true)
	t.Logf("Boris off: |chi|^2 at 500/1000/1500/2000 steps = %.4g %.4g %.4g %.4g", off[0], off[1], off[2], off[3])
	t.Logf("Boris on : |chi|^2 at 500/1000/1500/2000 steps = %.4g %.4g %.4g %.4g", on[0], on[1], on[2], on[3])
	if off[3] < 10*off[0] {
		t.Errorf("expected the explicit step to run away: %g -> %g", off[0], off[3])
	}
	if on[3] > 2*on[0] || math.IsNaN(on[3]) {
		t.Errorf("Boris should stay bounded: %g -> %g", on[0], on[3])
	}
}
EOF

p='init.goal'
s=open(p).read()
o = """// ChargedUniform fills space with a uniform complex wave turning at the rest
// mass frequency Omega0, which is a constant charge density of -sign e amp^2.
// The two components are a quarter cycle apart, as complex numbers always are;
// sign picks which way it turns, and so the sign of the charge.
func (ss *Sim) ChargedUniform(amp, sign float32) {
	ss.Fill(CabPosA, Both, amp)
	ss.Fill(CabVelB, Both, sign*ss.Params.Omega0*amp)
}"""
n = """// ChargedUniform fills space with a uniform complex wave turning at the rest
// mass frequency Omega0, which is a constant charge density of -sign e amp^2.
// The two components are a quarter cycle apart, as complex numbers always are;
// sign picks which way it turns, and so the sign of the charge.
//
// With Params.EM on, the local A0 is subtracted from the turning rate. A
// potential shifts the phase rate by -e A0 / hbar, so a wave genuinely at rest
// in that potential turns at Omega0 - e A0 / hbar. Leaving it out starts the
// wave in a superposition of the two frequencies present, and |chi|^2 beats
// instead of sitting still.
func (ss *Sim) ChargedUniform(amp, sign float32) {
	ss.Fill(CabPosA, Both, amp)
	om := ss.Params.Omega0
	if ss.Params.EM.IsFalse() {
		ss.Fill(CabVelB, Both, sign*om*amp)
		return
	}
	eoh := ss.Params.E / ss.Params.Hbar
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				v := sign * (om - eoh*State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, A0s, cur]) * amp
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, CabVelB, cur] += v
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, CabVelB, prv] += v
			}
		}
	}
}"""
assert o in s

a = s.index("// TestKGGaugeUniform")
n2 = '''// TestKGGaugeUniform: a uniform constant A0 is pure gauge -- it multiplies chi
// by a phase and changes no observable. Both |chi|^2 and the total charge must
// come out the same as with no field at all.
//
// The charge is the sharper half. Its free part alone is NOT invariant: the
// phase rotation adds to phi_b d(phi_a) - phi_a d(phi_b). The -e^2 A0 |chi|^2
// term in rho is exactly what cancels that, so this checks that the coupling
// term in the CHARGE matches the coupling term in the EQUATION.
//
// The field has to be set BEFORE the wave, because ChargedUniform reads A0 to
// get the turning rate right; start it at the free rate and the state is a
// superposition of the two frequencies, which beats and is not a gauge
// transform of anything.
func TestKGGaugeUniform(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 6
	run := func(a0 float32) (q, cc float64) {
		ss := kgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			if a0 != 0 {
				s.Params.EM.SetBool(true)
				s.Params.Update()
			}
			s.Fill(A0s, Both, a0)
			ChargeAtRest(s)
		})
		for range 200 {
			kgStepExt(ss)
		}
		return kgSum(sz, Charge), kgSum(sz, CabCC)
	}
	q0, cc0 := run(0)
	for _, a0 := range []float32{0.001, 0.005, 0.01} {
		q, cc := run(a0)
		t.Logf("A0 = %.3f (e A0 / hbar is %.2f of Omega0): charge %+.5f (%+.1e)   |chi|^2 %.5f (%+.1e)",
			a0, float64(a0)/float64(Params[0].Omega0), q, q/q0-1, cc, cc/cc0-1)
		if math.Abs(q/q0-1) > 1e-3 {
			t.Errorf("A0 = %g changed the charge by %.2e: a uniform A0 is pure gauge", a0, q/q0-1)
		}
		if math.Abs(cc/cc0-1) > 1e-3 {
			t.Errorf("A0 = %g changed |chi|^2 by %.2e", a0, cc/cc0-1)
		}
	}
}

// TestKGBorisStability: the A0 coupling turns the velocity (d phi_a, d phi_b)
// at rate 2 e A0 / hbar. An explicit step does not turn it, it spirals out, and
// the wave grows without bound -- the instability web/content/complex-kg.md
// describes and works around by updating the two components in sequence.
// Params.Boris applies the rotation exactly instead.
//
// A0 is chosen so e A0 / hbar is comparable to Omega0. Much smaller and the
// explicit step survives too; much larger and the single-particle equation is
// past the Klein regime anyway, where the potential exceeds the rest energy.
func TestKGBorisStability(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 6
	run := func(boris bool) (first, last float64) {
		ss := kgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Params.EM.SetBool(true)
			s.Params.Boris.SetBool(boris)
			s.Params.Update()
			s.Fill(A0s, Both, 0.03)
			ChargeAtRest(s)
		})
		kgStepExt(ss)
		first = kgSum(sz, CabCC)
		for range 2000 {
			kgStepExt(ss)
		}
		return first, kgSum(sz, CabCC)
	}
	f0, l0 := run(false)
	f1, l1 := run(true)
	t.Logf("Boris off: |chi|^2 %.4g -> %.4g  (x%.3g)", f0, l0, l0/f0)
	t.Logf("Boris on : |chi|^2 %.4g -> %.4g  (x%.3g)", f1, l1, l1/f1)
	if l0 < 50*f0 {
		t.Errorf("expected the explicit step to run away: %g -> %g", f0, l0)
	}
	if l1 > 2*f1 || math.IsNaN(l1) {
		t.Errorf("Boris should stay bounded: %g -> %g", f1, l1)
	}
}
'''

Complex KG with EM coupling is in — 40 tests pass, 14 validations, everything builds.

## What I built

Following the Dirac/electroweak precedent, `CabStates` is now based on `EMStates`, so the complex wave and the Maxwell field share state: the wave reads the A₀/A it's pushed by and writes the ρ/J that drive them. `Params.EM` gates it (default off, so Schrödinger/Spinfield are unchanged), and `StepRun` runs `MaxwellKernel` first when it's on.

The kernel implements your `complex-kg.md` equations as written — I checked them against the covariant derivative expansion and they're self-consistent, including the relative $1/c^2$ between ρ and J that makes continuity balance.

```
free packet: total charge 5.842599e+03, drift over 2000 steps 9.89e-03 (relative 1.69e-06)
ChargeAtRest      total charge -216.00000 (want -216.00000)
ChargeAtRestAnti  total charge +216.00000 (want +216.00000)
```

Charge conserved to **1.7e-6** with no field, and the rest-state charge hits the analytic $-e|\chi|^2$ exactly. Same wave, opposite rotation sense, opposite charge — antimatter in the only sense this equation knows.

Local continuity converges cleanly:

```
wavelength  4: RMS(d rho/dt + div J) / RMS(div J) = 0.3515
wavelength  8:                                      0.0613   (5.7x)
wavelength 16:                                      0.0087   (7.0x)
```

Gauge invariance under a uniform A₀ — the sharp test, since it checks that the $-e^2A_0|\chi|^2$ term in ρ matches the coupling term in the equation:

```
A0 = 0.001: charge -216.00196 (+9.1e-06)   |chi|^2 216.20697 (-7.1e-05)
A0 = 0.010: charge -216.01614 (+7.5e-05)   |chi|^2 216.10374 (-5.5e-04)
```

## On the instability in the write-up

`Params.Boris` supersedes the sequential-update fix, and it's the same machinery as the electroweak Higgs. In a 1/r potential:

```
1/r peak 0.05:  explicit |chi|^2 2715 -> 8.602e+38 (x3.17e+35)
                Boris    |chi|^2 2713 -> 3592 (x1.32), charge varies by 0.08%
1/r peak 0.20:  explicit |chi|^2 2627 -> NaN
                Boris    |chi|^2 2615 -> 3420 (x1.31), charge varies by 0.39%
```

**Two corrections to the write-up's account, and I'd hold the second loosely.**

First, the instability is not intrinsic to the coupling — it's an explicit integrator failing to rotate. The A₀ term turns $(\dot\phi_a, \dot\phi_b)$ at rate $2eA_0/\hbar$; Boris applies that rotation exactly and it's bounded. So the passage suggesting the required symmetry-breaking might map onto weak-force chirality is, I think, reading physics into an integration artifact. The rotation is real and stays; only the spiral goes away.

Second, part of it was an initial condition. A potential shifts the phase rate to $\Omega_0 - eA_0/\hbar$; start at the free rate and the state is a superposition of two frequencies that beats. With a *uniform* A₀ and the corrected start, the explicit scheme is perfectly stable — the runaway needs a field the wave is genuinely being pushed around by. I've made `ChargedUniform` read the local A₀ so the configs start in the right state.

I'd flag that as "worth re-deriving yourself" rather than settled: it came out of my tests, and the write-up describes long runs I haven't reproduced.

Also, the charge drift the write-up reports is now **0.08%**, not the large excursions in that figure — likely the same two causes.

## One thing I found along the way

`MovingWavePacket` sets its velocity from hand-fitted constants (`vamp`, `vwavelength`, `vphase`, `veloff`, with a regime switch at wavelength > 20) tuned for massless waves. The packet it makes is not a KG eigenstate — it splits. That was my continuity test's first failure. `ChargedPacketConfig` now builds from `SlabPacket` at the exact lattice frequency instead. The old function is still there and still used elsewhere; it may be worth the same treatment.

## Configs and stats

"Charge At Rest", "Charge At Rest Anti", "Charged Packet" in the GUI menu, plus `KleinGordonCStats` (total charge, |χ|², energy, group velocity) wired into `waves.go`. `KGCShouldDisplay` exposes E, Mu0, EM, Boris, A0NoWave.

The scaling to watch when you go to Dirac: $eA_0/\hbar$ vs $\Omega_0 = mc^2/\hbar$. At defaults $\Omega_0 = 0.031$, so with $e = 1$ a field above ~0.03 is past the Klein regime, where single-particle KG stops meaning anything and both integrators eventually fail.
